↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

On the Logos prologue, Cyril resists any temporal reading of 'in the beginning was the Word': the Word is co-eternal with the Father, not produced as the first effect of the Father's will. Cyril's Miaphysite formula — 'one nature of the incarnate Word' — anchors the Tewahedo christological tradition; the Ethiopian Liturgy of St Cyril ('Anaphora of Cyril of Alexandria') is one of the principal eucharistic prayers of the Ethiopian Church to this day.

↩ ◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria De Incarnatione Verbi §1 (c. 350 AD)

'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' — Athanasius marks Jn 1:1 as the Johannine PROEM that the entire De Incarnatione exposits. The triad of predicates is irreducible: ēn (was — eternal continuous-existence, not egeneto came-to-be); pros ton theon (with God — relationally-distinct from the Father); theos ēn (was God — ontologically-identical-essence with the Father). The triad names the eternal-Word's eternal-existence + eternal-distinction + eternal-divinity in one breath. Athanasius's anti-Arian polemic stands or falls on this verse: the Word never came-to-be (no 'there was a time when he was not' — the Arian-slogan ēn pote hote ouk ēn is the exact contradiction of ēn here). Tewahedo Logos-theology cites Jn 1:1 + Heb 1:1-3 + Col 1:15-17 as the irreducible-Logos-triad of biblical-Christology.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). VERSION a translation of the holy Scriptures. This word is not found in the Bible, nevertheless, as frequent references are made in this work to various ancient as well as modern versions, it is fitting that some brief account should be given of the most important of these. These versions are important helps to the right interpretation of the Word. (See SAMARITAN PENTATEUCH.) 1. The Targums. After the return from the Captivity, the Jews, no longer familiar with the old Hebrew, required that their Scriptures should be translated for them into the Chaldaic or Aramaic language and interpreted. These translations and paraphrases were at first oral, but they were afterwards reduced to writing, and thus targums, i.e., “versions” or “translations”, have come down to us. The chief of these are, (1.) The Onkelos Targum, i.e., the targum of Akelas=Aquila, a targum so called to give it greater popularity by comparing it with the Greek translation of Aquila mentioned below. This targum originated about the second century after Christ. (2.) The targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel comes next to that of Onkelos in respect of age and value. It is more a paraphrase on the Prophets, however, than a translation. Both of these targums issued from the Jewish school which then flourished at Babylon. 2. The Greek Versions. (1.) The oldest of these is the Septuagint, usually quoted as the LXX. The origin of this the most important of all the versions is involved in much obscurity. It derives its name from the popular notion that seventy-two translators were employed on it by the direction of Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Egypt, and that it was accomplished in seventy-two days, for the use of the Jews residing in that country. There is no historical warrant for this notion. It is, however, an established fact that this version was made at Alexandria; that it was begun about 280 B.C., and finished about 200 or 150 B.C.; that it was the work of a number of translators who differed greatly both in their knowledge of Hebrew and of Greek; and that from the earliest times it has borne the name of “The Septuagint”, i.e., The Seventy. THE PAGE BELOW CONTAINS SPECIMENS OF VARIOUS VERSIONS Codex ALEXANDRINUS: Fifth Century. — John 1:1. Ev arch nv o logov kai o logov h~ prov tov Qªeoºn kai Qªeoºn hn o logov Codex CLAROMONTANUS: Sixth Century; Greek Text. — 1 Cor. 13:8. h> ajga>ph oJude’pote eJkpi>ptei Codex LAUDIANUS: Sixth Century; Greek Text. — Acts 20:28. thn ekklhsian tou kªurioºu Codex PURPUREUS: Sixth Century, — John 15:20. tou logou ou Codex AMIATINUS, A.D. 541: the oldest known MS. of the Vulgate, — Acts 7:6. Loctus est autem d[eu]s Codex COLBERTINUS: Eleventh Century; the “Queen of the Cursives”, — Luke 1:8, 9 xei thv eujsebe(?)i>av musth>rion? oJ Qªeo<ºv eJfanerw>qh ejn sar ki>? w]fqh agge>loiv Codex LEICESTRESIS: Fourteenth Century. — 1 Timothy 3:16 th~v eujsebe(?)i>av musth>rion? oJ Qªeo>ºv ejfanerw>qh ejn sar ki>? ejdikaiw>qh ejdikaiw>qh ejn pneu>mati? w]fqh ajgge>loiv of a number of translators who differed greatly both in their knowledge of Hebrew and of Greek; and that from the earliest times it has borne the name of “The Septuagint”, i.e., The Seventy. “This version, with all its defects, must be of the greatest interest, (a) as preserving evidence for the text far more ancient than the oldest Hebrew manuscripts; (b) as the means by which the Greek Language was wedded to Hebrew thought; (c) as the source of the great majority of quotations from the Old Testament by writers of the New Testament. (2.) The New Testament manuscripts fall into two divisions, Uncials, written in Greek capitals, with no distinction at all between the different words, and very little even between the different lines; and Cursives, in small Greek letters, and with divisions of words and lines. The change between the two kinds of Greek writing took place about the tenth century. Only five manuscripts of the New Testament approaching to completeness are more ancient than this dividing date. The first, numbered A, is the Alexandrian manuscript. Though brought to this country by Cyril Lucar, patriarch of Constantinople, as a present to Charles I., it is believed that it was written, not in that capital, but in Alexandria; whence its title. It is now dated in the fifth century A.D. The second, known as B, is the Vatican manuscript. (See VATICANUS.) The Third, C, or the Ephraem manuscript, was so called because it was written over the writings of Ephraem, a Syrian theological author, a practice very common in the days when writing materials were scarce and dear. It is believed that it belongs to the fifth century, and perhaps a slightly earlier period of it than the manuscript A. The fourth, D, or the manuscript of Beza, was so called because it belonged to the reformer Beza, who found it in the monastery of St. Irenaeus at Lyons in 1562 A.D. It is imperfect, and is dated in the sixth century. The fifth (called Aleph) is the Sinaitic manuscript. (See SINAITICUS.) 3. The Syriac Versions. (See SYRIAC.) 4. The Latin Versions. A Latin version of the Scriptures, called the “Old Latin,” which originated in North Africa, was in common use in the time of Tertullian (A.D. 150). Of this there appear to have been various copies or recensions made. That made in Italy, and called the Itala, was reckoned the most accurate. This translation of the Old Testament seems to have been made not from the original Hebrew but from the LXX. This version became greatly corrupted by repeated transcription, and to remedy the evil Jerome (A.D. 329-420) was requested by Damasus, the bishop of Rome, to undertake a complete revision of it. It met with opposition at first, but was at length, in the seventh century, recognized as the “Vulgate” version. It appeared in a printed from about A.D. 1455, the first book that ever issued from the press. The Council of Trent (1546) declared it “authentic.” It subsequently underwent various revisions, but that which was executed (1592) under the sanction of Pope Clement VIII. was adopted as the basis of all subsequent editions. It is regarded as the sacred original in the Roman Catholic Church. All modern European versions have been more or less influenced by the Vulgate. This version reads ipsa instead of ipse in Genesis 3:15, “She shall bruise thy head.” 5. There are several other ancient versions which are of importance for Biblical critics, but which we need not mention particularly, such as the Ethiopic, in the fourth century, from the LXX.; two Egyptian versions, about the fourth century, the Memphitic, circulated in Lower Egypt, and the Thebaic, designed for Upper Egypt, both from the Greek; the Gothic, written in the German language, but with the Greek alphabet, by Ulphilas (died A.D. 388), of which only fragments of the Old Testament remain; the Armenian, about A.D. 400; and the Slavonic, in the ninth century, for ancient Moravia. Other ancient versions, as the Arabic, the Persian, and the Anglo-Saxon, may be mentioned. 6. The history of the English versions begins properly with Wyckliffe. Portions, however, of the Scriptures were rendered into Saxon (as the Gospel according to John, by Bede, A.D. 735), and also into English (by Orme, called the “Ormulum,” a portion of the Gospels and of the Acts in the form of a metrical paraphrase, toward the close of the seventh century), long before Wyckliffe; but it is to him that the honour belongs of having first rendered the whole Bible into English (A.D. 1380). This version was made from the Vulgate, and renders Genesis 3:15 after that Version, “She shall trede thy head.” This was followed by Tyndale’s translation (1525-1531); Miles Coverdale’s (1535-1553); Thomas Matthew’s (1537), really, however, the work of John Rogers, the first martyr under the reign of Queen Mary. This was properly the first Authorized Version, Henry VIII. having ordered a copy of it to be got for every church. This took place in less than a year after Tyndale was martyred for the crime of translating the Scriptures. In 1539 Richard Taverner published a revised edition of Matthew’s Bible. The Great Bible, so called from its great size, called also Cranmer’s Bible, was published in 1539 and 1568. In the strict sense, the “Great Bible” is “the only authorized version; for the Bishops’ Bible and the present Bible [the A.V.] never had the formal sanction of royal authority.” Next in order was the Geneva version (1557-1560); the Bishops’ Bible (1568); the Rheims and Douai versions, under Roman Catholic auspices (1582, 1609); the Authorized Version (1611); and the Revised Version of the New Testament in 1880 and of the Old Testament in 1884.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). WORD , THE (Gr. Logos), one of the titles of our Lord, found only in the writings of John (John 1:1-14; 1 John 1:1; Revelation 19:13). As such, Christ is the revealer of God. His office is to make God known. “No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him” (John 1:18). This title designates the divine nature of Christ. As the Word, he “was in the beginning” and “became flesh.” “The Word was with God “ and “was God,” and was the Creator of all things (comp. Psalm 33: 6; 107:20; 119:89; 147:18; Isaiah 40:8).

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'All things were made through Him' Cyril takes as a comprehensive denial of any creaturely status in the Son: the Word is not among things made, but is Himself the Maker. Cyril notes the deliberate Johannine choice of 'di' autou' (through Him) rather than 'hyp' autou' (by Him): the preposition does not subordinate the Son to the Father (as Arians read) but expresses the eternal Trinitarian order, the Father acting through the Son as His co-eternal Word. The Tewahedo Anaphora of the Apostles preserves this verse's anti-Arian cadence in its prayer of consecration: 'through whom all things were made'.

↩ ◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos II.21 (c. 350 AD)

'All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made' — Athanasius marks panta di' autou egeneto, kai chōris autou egeneto oude hen ho gegonen (all-things came-into-being THROUGH him, and apart-from-him came-into-being not-one-thing of-what-came-into-being) as the CREATIONAL-ASYMMETRY anchor against Arian inclusion-of-the-Son-in-creation. The Word is the THROUGH-WHOM-of-creation (di' autou), not part-of-what-came-into-being. The repeated egeneto / egeneto / gegonen (came-into-being) applies to creation-creatures, NEVER to the Word (Jn 1:1 — ēn ho Logos, was-the-Word, imperfect-tense-eternal-being, contrasts with egeneto came-into-being). The grammatical-distinction is decisive: the Word is, all-other-things came-to-be.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'In Him was life, and the life was the light of men' Cyril reads as the Son's eternal possession of life — not life received, but life owned. The Word is the source of life for every creature that lives, and the life He bestows is also light: the rational illumination that distinguishes humanity. Cyril builds toward his pneumatological argument: this life-and-light shared by the Word with humanity is the prefiguring of the Spirit's later indwelling. The Tewahedo baptismal liturgy preserves this connection: candidates are addressed as those returning to the Light-of-the-Word that was theirs in creation.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'The light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not' Cyril reads as the post-lapsarian condition of humanity: the Word's light continues to shine (creation has not extinguished it) but the darkness of human sin and demonic deception fails to receive it. The Greek 'katelaben' carries the double sense of 'comprehend' and 'overcome' — Cyril preserves both: the darkness neither understands the Light nor masters it. The verse becomes for Cyril the Christological hinge: the Word continues to shine in every conscience even before the Incarnation, and continues afterward despite humanity's refusal.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'The true Light, which lighteth every man, was coming into the world' Cyril reads against the Manichaean and gnostic readings of his day: the Word's illumination is universal, not restricted to a spiritual elite. Every rational creature receives some measure of the Word's light — this is what makes humanity capable of recognizing Christ when He comes in the flesh. Cyril notes the imperfect tense 'was coming' (erchomenon) as anticipating the Incarnation: the eternal illumination has always been preparing humanity for the historical advent of the Word made flesh.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'He came unto His own, and His own received Him not' Cyril reads with characteristic precision: 'His own' (ta idia) refers in the first sense to the Jewish people whom He had elected as His covenant possession, but in the broader sense to all humanity whom He had created. The double rejection (covenantal + creational) frames the Incarnation as the Maker's return to a world that has forgotten Him. For Cyril this is no Marcionite cancellation of Israel but the painful pathos of God's faithfulness meeting human refusal — the verse becomes the textual root of medieval Tewahedo homiletic readings of the prophetic ministry.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'As many as received Him, to them He gave the right (exousia) to become children of God' Cyril reads as the gift of adoptive sonship through participation in the natural Sonship of the Word. The 'exousia' is not merely permission but operative power — divine grace that effects what it confers. Cyril here begins his exposition of theosis: humans become 'children' (tekna, lower than 'huios') not by nature but by gift, through the Spirit's adoption that conforms them to Christ's image. This adoptive doctrine is foundational for the Tewahedo understanding of baptism as the moment of theosis-by-participation.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God' Cyril reads as the threefold negation of every natural-genealogical claim to divine sonship: Jewish ancestry (blood), human reproductive desire (will of flesh), patriarchal authority (will of man) all fail to constitute the new birth. Only the Spirit's begetting through baptism produces children of God. Cyril notes that this verse is the conceptual seed of the later baptismal regeneration doctrine — the new birth is Trinitarian in structure (the Father's gift, the Son's mediation, the Spirit's effecting) and ecclesial in setting (administered in the Church's baptismal economy).

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'The Word became flesh' is, for Cyril, the dogmatic foundation of the Miaphysite confession received by Tewahedo: one incarnate nature of the Word, indivisibly united from two natures (divine and human) without confusion. Against the Nestorian reading that finds two persons or two natures-after-union, Cyril insists the union is hypostatic and indivisible. The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors Cyril on the 3rd of Hamlē for this defense.

↩ ◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria De Incarnatione Verbi §8 (c. 350 AD)

'And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth' — Athanasius marks ho Logos sarx egeneto (the Word became flesh) as the SINGLE most important verse for the entire incarnational-treatise. The egeneto (became) is genuine becoming — not Docetic-appearing, not Arian-creature-clothing, not Nestorian-association-with. The Word remained-what-he-was (eternal-divine-Logos) and BECAME-what-he-was-not (genuine-human-sarx). The eskēnōsen (dwelt — literally 'tabernacled') connects to the OT shekinah-dwelling and to Jn 2:21 ('he spake of the temple of his body'). The doxan-as-of-monogenous (glory-of-only-begotten) is the visible-Shekinah-glory of the incarnate-Word that Peter, James, John see at the Transfiguration (Mt 17:1-8, 2 Pet 1:16-18). This is Athanasius's signature-verse: DI §54's famous 'He was made man that we might be made God' is the soteriological-corollary of Jn 1:14's incarnational-fact. The Tewahedo Lǝdat-creed cites Jn 1:14 first among the Johannine prologue verses.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'No man hath seen God at any time; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He hath declared Him' is for Cyril the dogmatic statement of the Son's unique revelatory office. 'In the bosom of the Father' (eis ton kolpon tou Patros) Cyril reads not spatially but as expressing intimate co-substantiality and eternal mutual indwelling. The Son's revelation is not derivative testimony but the Father's self-disclosure in His own Word. Against Eunomian rationalism (which claimed direct knowledge of the divine essence), Cyril here grounds Christian epistemology in the Son's mediation: we know the Father only through the Son who eternally knows Him.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

On John the Baptist's self-identification as 'the voice of one crying in the wilderness' (citing Isa 40:3), Cyril develops the patristic distinction between Voice (phone) and Word (logos): the Baptist is the audible preparation for the eternal Word's manifestation. The Voice is heard, then ceases; the Word abides forever. The 'wilderness' Cyril reads typologically: not merely the Judean desert but the spiritual barrenness of pre-Incarnational humanity awaiting the Word's coming. The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors the Baptist as the 'lamp of Christ' on the 30th of Hidar, preserving this Voice-Word distinction in its liturgical hymnody.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BETHABARA house of the ford, a place on the east bank of the Jordan, where John was baptizing (John 1:28). It may be identical with Bethbarah, the ancient ford of Jordan of which the men of Ephraim took possession (Judges 7:24). The Revised Version reads “Bethany beyond Jordan.” It was the great ford, and still bears the name of “the ford,” Makhadhet ‘Abarah, “the ford of crossing over,” about 25 miles from Nazareth. (See BETHBARAH.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BETHANY house of dates. (1.) The Revised Version in John 1:28 has this word instead of Bethabara, on the authority of the oldest manuscripts. It appears to have been the name of a place on the east of Jordan. (2.) A village on the south-eastern slope of the Mount of Olives (Mark 11:1), about 2 miles east of Jerusalem, on the road to Jericho. It derived its name from the number of palm-trees which grew there. It was the residence of Lazarus and his sisters. It is frequently mentioned in connection with memorable incidents in the life of our Lord (Matthew 21:17; 26:6; Mark 11:11, 12; 14:3; Luke 24:50; John 11:1; 12:1). It is now known by the name of el-Azariyeh, i.e., “place of Lazarus,” or simply Lazariyeh. Seen from a distance, the village has been described as “remarkably beautiful, the perfection of retirement and repose, of seclusion and lovely peace.” Now a mean village, containing about twenty families.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world' Cyril reads as the typological climax of the entire Hebrew sacrificial economy: the Paschal lamb of Exodus, the lambs of the daily burnt offering, the Isaianic lamb led to the slaughter — all converge in the Baptist's pointing finger. The 'taketh away' (airon) Cyril stresses as present-tense ongoing action: the Lamb's atoning work is not a single historical moment but the perpetual offering perpetually applied through the Church's eucharistic representation. This sacrificial-eucharistic reading is foundational to the Tewahedo Anaphora's offertory prayers.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending and remaining (menon) on Him' Cyril reads with characteristic pneumatological depth: the Spirit's *remaining* (not just descending) distinguishes Christ from all the prophets, on whom the Spirit had come and departed. The Spirit's permanent indwelling of the incarnate Word is the source of every subsequent gift of the Spirit to humanity — what Christ possesses by nature, He communicates to the baptized by participation. Cyril here grounds his entire pneumatology in the Jordan event: the Holy Spirit's mission to the Church flows from His abiding upon the Son.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ANDREW manliness, a Greek name; one of the apostles of our Lord. He was of Bethsaida in Galilee (John 1:44), and was the brother of Simon Peter (Matthew 4:18; 10:2). On one occasion John the Baptist, whose disciple he then was, pointing to Jesus, said, “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1:40); and Andrew, hearing him, immediately became a follower of Jesus, the first of his disciples. After he had been led to recognize Jesus as the Messiah, his first care was to bring also his brother Simon to Jesus. The two brothers seem to have after this pursued for a while their usual calling as fishermen, and did not become the stated attendants of the Lord till after John’s imprisonment (Matthew 4:18, 19; Mark 1:16, 17). Very little is related of Andrew. He was one of the confidential disciples (John 6:8; 12:22), and with Peter, James, and John inquired of our Lord privately regarding his future coming (Mark 13:3). He was present at the feeding of the five thousand (John 6:9), and he introduced the Greeks who desired to see Jesus (John 12:22); but of his subsequent history little is known. It is noteworthy that Andrew thrice brings others to Christ, (1) Peter; (2) the lad with the loaves; and (3) certain Greeks. These incidents may be regarded as a key to his character.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PHILIP lover of horses. (1.) One of the twelve apostles; a native of Bethsaida, “the city of Andrew and Peter” (John 1:44). He readily responded to the call of Jesus when first addressed to him (43), and forthwith brought Nathanael also to Jesus (45,46). He seems to have held a prominent place among the apostles (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; John 6:5-7; 12:21, 22; 14:8, 9; Acts 1:13). Of his later life nothing is certainly known. He is said to have preached in Phrygia, and to have met his death at Hierapolis. (2.) One of the “seven” (Acts 6:5), called also “the evangelist” (21:8, 9). He was one of those who were “scattered abroad” by the persecution that arose on the death of Stephen. He went first to Samaria, where he laboured as an evangelist with much success (8:5-13). While he was there he received a divine command to proceed toward the south, along the road leading from Jerusalem to Gaza. These towns were connected by two roads. The one Philip was directed to take was that which led through Hebron, and thence through a district little inhabited, and hence called “desert.” As he travelled along this road he was overtaken by a chariot in which sat a man of Ethiopia, the eunuch or chief officer of Queen Candace, who was at that moment reading, probably from the Septuagint version, a portion of the prophecies of Isaiah (53:6,7). Philip entered into conversation with him, and expounded these verses, preaching to him the glad tidings of the Saviour. The eunuch received the message and believed, and was forthwith baptized, and then “went on his way rejoicing.” Philip was instantly caught away by the Spirit after the baptism, and the eunuch saw him no more. He was next found at Azotus, whence he went forth in his evangelistic work till he came to Caesarea. He is not mentioned again for about twenty years, when he is still found at Caesarea (Acts 21:8) when Paul and his companions were on the way to Jerusalem. He then finally disappears from the page of history. (3.) Mentioned only in connection with the imprisonment of John the Baptist (Matthew 14:3; Mark 6:17; Luke 3:19). He was the son of Herod the Great, and the first husband of Herodias, and the father of Salome. (See HEROD PHILIP I.) (4.) The “tetrarch of Ituraea” (Luke 3:1); a son of Herod the Great, and brother of Herod Antipas. The city of Caesarea-Philippi was named partly after him (Matthew 16:13; Mark 8:27). (See HEROD PHILIP II.)

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man' Cyril reads as the Christological fulfillment of Jacob's ladder vision (Gen 28:12): the incarnate Christ IS the ladder uniting heaven and earth in His own Person. The angels' bidirectional movement signifies the restored communication between divinity and creation through the Word made flesh. Cyril notes that this is the first explicit messianic self-identification in John's Gospel ('Son of man') and that it grounds the entire subsequent series of theophanic 'I am' sayings.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CANA reedy, a town of Galilee, near Capernaum. Here our Lord wrought his first miracle, the turning of water into wine (John 2:1-11; 4:46). It is also mentioned as the birth-place of Nathanael (21:2). It is not mentioned in the Old Testament. It has been identified with the modern Kana el-Jelil, also called Khurbet Kana, a place 8 or 9 miles north of Nazareth. Others have identified it with Kefr Kenna, which lies on the direct road to the Sea of Galilee, about 5 miles north-east of Nazareth, and 12 in a direct course from Tiberias. It is called “Cana of Galilee,” to distinguish it from Cana of Asher (Joshua 19:28).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MARRIAGE-FEASTS (John 2:1-11) “lasted usually for a whole week; but the cost of such prolonged rejoicing is very small in the East. The guests sit round the great bowl or bowls on the floor, the meal usually consisting of a lamb or kid stewed in rice or barley. The most honoured guests sit nearest, others behind; and all in eating dip their hand into the one smoking mound, pieces of the thin bread, bent together, serving for spoons when necessary. After the first circle have satisfied themselves, those lower in honour sit down to the rest, the whole company being men, for women are never seen at a feast. Water is poured on the hands before eating; and this is repeated when the meal closes, the fingers having first been wiped on pieces of bread, which, after serving the same purpose as table-napkins with us, are thrown on the ground to be eaten by any dog that may have stolen in from the streets through the ever-open door, or picked up by those outside when gathered and tossed out to them (Matthew 15:27; Mark 7:28). Rising from the ground and retiring to the seats round the walls, the guests then sit down cross-legged and gossip, or listen to recitals, or puzzle over riddles, light being scantily supplied by a small lamp or two, or if the night be chilly, by a smouldering fire of weeds kindled in the middle of the room, perhaps in a brazier, often in a hole in the floor. As to the smoke, it escapes as it best may; but indeed there is little of it, though enough to blacken the water or wine or milk skins hung up on pegs on the wall. (Comp. Psalm 119:83.) To some such marriage-feast Jesus and his five disciples were invited at Cana of Galilee.” Geikie’s Life of Christ. (See CANA.)

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Cyril carefully defends Christ's address to His mother at Cana ('Woman, what have I to do with thee?') against any reading that would imply disrespect. 'Woman' (gynai) is for Cyril a formal address of honor, not familiarity-refused; the question is rhetorical, situating the miracle within His Father's appointed timing rather than maternal pressure. Mary's authority remains intact (she immediately directs the servants to obey Christ) — the verse establishes the principle that Christ's miracles proceed from the Father's will, not human request, even when that human is His own mother. Tewahedo Marian veneration preserves this delicate balance.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Fill the waterpots with water' Cyril reads as the typological pivot of the entire Cana sign: Christ deliberately requires human cooperation (the servants' labor of filling) before the divine transformation. The six stone waterpots — used for Jewish purification rites — Cyril reads as the six days of creation (the imperfect order awaiting completion), or as the Old Covenant's purification economy awaiting Christ's New Covenant fulfillment. The water-to-wine transformation prefigures the eucharistic transformation: the elements remain (water/bread), but their inner reality is changed by Christ's word.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

On 'This beginning of miracles did Jesus' Cyril notes the programmatic placement: a wedding-feast miracle inaugurates the public ministry, signaling that Christ's mission is nuptial in character — He has come to wed humanity to divinity in His own flesh. 'Manifested forth His glory' (ephanerōsen tēn doxan autou) Cyril reads as the proleptic revelation of the cross's glory: the Cana glory and the Calvary glory are one glory, the glory of the eternal Word visible in His incarnate works. The disciples' belief that follows is the first-fruits of the entire Church's faith.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). TEMPLE , HEROD’S The temple erected by the exiles on their return from Babylon had stood for about five hundred years, when Herod the Great became king of Judea. The building had suffered considerably from natural decay as well as from the assaults of hostile armies, and Herod, desirous of gaining the favour of the Jews, proposed to rebuild it. This offer was accepted, and the work was begun (B.C. 18), and carried out at great labour and expense, and on a scale of surpassing splendour. The main part of the building was completed in ten years, but the erection of the outer courts and the embellishment of the whole were carried on during the entire period of our Lord’s life on earth (John 2:16, 19-21), and the temple was completed only A.D. 65. But it was not long permitted to exist. Within forty years after our Lord’s crucifixion, his prediction of its overthrow was accomplished (Luke 19: 41-44). The Roman legions took the city of Jerusalem by storm, and notwithstanding the strenuous efforts Titus made to preserve the temple, his soldiers set fire to it in several places, and it was utterly destroyed (A.D. 70), and was never rebuilt. Several remains of Herod’s stately temple have by recent explorations been brought to light. It had two courts, one intended for the Israelites only, and the other, a large outer court, called “the court of the Gentiles,” intended for the use of strangers of all nations. These two courts were separated by a low wall, as Josephus states, some 4 1/2 feet high, with thirteen openings. Along the top of this dividing wall, at regular intervals, were placed pillars bearing in Greek an inscription to the effect that no stranger was, on the pain of death, to pass from the court of the Gentiles into that of the Jews. At the entrance to a graveyard at the north-western angle of the Haram wall, a stone was discovered by M. Ganneau in 1871, built into the wall, bearing the following inscription in Greek capitals: “No stranger is to enter within the partition wall and enclosure around the sanctuary. Whoever is caught will be responsible to himself for his death, which will ensue.” There can be no doubt that the stone thus discovered was one of those originally placed on the boundary wall which separated the Jews from the Gentiles, of which Josephus speaks. It is of importance to notice that the word rendered “sanctuary” in the inscription was used in a specific sense of the inner court, the court of the Israelites, and is the word rendered “temple” in John 2:15 and Acts 21:28, 29. When Paul speaks of the middle wall of partition (Ephesians 2:14), he probably makes allusion to this dividing wall. Within this partition wall stood the temple proper, consisting of, (1) the court of the women, 8 feet higher than the outer court; (2) 10 feet higher than this court was the court of Israel; (3) the court of the priests, again 3 feet higher; and lastly (4) the temple floor, 8 feet above that; thus in all 29 feet above the level of the outer court. The summit of Mount Moriah, on which the temple stood, is now occupied by the Haram esh-Sherif, i.e., “the sacred enclosure.” This enclosure is about 1,500 feet from north to south, with a breadth of about 1,000 feet, covering in all a space of about 35 acres. About the centre of the enclosure is a raised platform, 16 feet above the surrounding space, and paved with large stone slabs, on which stands the Mohammedan mosque called Kubbet es-Sahkra i.e., the “Dome of the Rock,” or the Mosque of Omar. This mosque covers the site of Solomon’s temple. In the centre of the dome there is a bare, projecting rock, the highest part of Moriah (q.v.), measuring 60 feet by 40, standing 6 feet above the floor of the mosque, called the sahkra, i.e., “rock.” Over this rock the altar of burnt-offerings stood. It was the threshing-floor of Araunah the Jebusite. The exact position on this “sacred enclosure” which the temple occupied has not been yet definitely ascertained. Some affirm that Herod’s temple covered the site of Solomon’s temple and palace, and in addition enclosed a square of 300 feet at the south-western angle. The temple courts thus are supposed to have occupied the southern portion of the “enclosure,” forming in all a square of more than 900 feet. It is argued by others that Herod’s temple occupied a square of 600 feet at the south-west of the “enclosure.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MIRACLE an event in the external world brought about by the immediate agency or the simple volition of God, operating without the use of means capable of being discerned by the senses, and designed to authenticate the divine commission of a religious teacher and the truth of his message (John 2:18; Matthew 12:38). It is an occurrence at once above nature and above man. It shows the intervention of a power that is not limited by the laws either of matter or of mind, a power interrupting the fixed laws which govern their movements, a supernatural power. “The suspension or violation of the laws of nature involved in miracles is nothing more than is constantly taking place around us. One force counteracts another: vital force keeps the chemical laws of matter in abeyance; and muscular force can control the action of physical force. When a man raises a weight from the ground, the law of gravity is neither suspended nor violated, but counteracted by a stronger force. The same is true as to the walking of Christ on the water and the swimming of iron at the command of the prophet. The simple and grand truth that the universe is not under the exclusive control of physical forces, but that everywhere and always there is above, separate from and superior to all else, an infinite personal will, not superseding, but directing and controlling all physical causes, acting with or without them.” God ordinarily effects his purpose through the agency of second causes; but he has the power also of effecting his purpose immediately and without the intervention of second causes, i.e., of invading the fixed order, and thus of working miracles. Thus we affirm the possibility of miracles, the possibility of a higher hand intervening to control or reverse nature’s ordinary movements. In the New Testament these four Greek words are principally used to designate miracles: (1.) Semeion, a “sign”, i.e., an evidence of a divine commission; an attestation of a divine message (Matthew 12:38, 39; 16:1, 4; Mark 8:11; Luke 11:16; 23:8; John 2:11, 18, 23; Acts 6:8, etc.); a token of the presence and working of God; the seal of a higher power. (2.) Terata, “wonders;” wonder-causing events; portents; producing astonishment in the beholder (Acts 2:19). (3.) Dunameis, “might works;” works of superhuman power (Acts 2:22; Romans 15:19; 2 Thessalonians 2:9); of a new and higher power. (4.) Erga, “works;” the works of Him who is “wonderful in working” (John 5:20, 36). Miracles are seals of a divine mission. The sacred writers appealed to them as proofs that they were messengers of God. Our Lord also appealed to miracles as a conclusive proof of his divine mission (John 5:20, 36; 10:25, 38). Thus, being out of the common course of nature and beyond the power of man, they are fitted to convey the impression of the presence and power of God. Where miracles are there certainly God is. The man, therefore, who works a miracle affords thereby clear proof that he comes with the authority of God; they are his credentials that he is God’s messenger. The teacher points to these credentials, and they are a proof that he speaks with the authority of God. He boldly says, “God bears me witness, both with signs and wonders, and with divers miracles.” The credibility of miracles is established by the evidence of the senses on the part of those who are witnesses of them, and to all others by the testimony of such witnesses. The witnesses were competent, and their testimony is trustworthy. Unbelievers, following Hume, deny that any testimony can prove a miracle, because they say miracles are impossible. We have shown that miracles are possible, and surely they can be borne witness to. Surely they are credible when we have abundant and trustworthy evidence of their occurrence. They are credible just as any facts of history well authenticated are credible. Miracles, it is said, are contrary to experience. Of course they are contrary to our experience, but that does not prove that they were contrary to the experience of those who witnessed them. We believe a thousand facts, both of history and of science, that are contrary to our experience, but we believe them on the ground of competent testimony. An atheist or a pantheist must, as a matter of course, deny the possibility of miracles; but to one who believes in a personal God, who in his wisdom may see fit to interfere with the ordinary processes of nature, miracles are not impossible, nor are they incredible. (See LIST OF MIRACLES, Appendix.)

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up' is for Cyril a Christological saying of central importance: the temple in question is not Herod's structure but Christ's body, and the active agent of the Resurrection is the Son Himself ('I will raise it up' — egerō auton). Against subordinationist readings that would make the Resurrection a passive event done TO Christ by the Father, Cyril insists on the Son's active agency: the Word raises His own assumed humanity through the divine power that is His own by nature. This is the dogmatic root of the Tewahedo Easter Anaphora's doxology of the Risen Christ as agent of His own resurrection.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

John's interpretive aside — 'He spake of the temple of His body' — provides Cyril his exegetical warrant for body-as-temple typology that runs throughout his John commentary. The Old Covenant temple (with its court of Gentiles, holy place, holy of holies) prefigures the structure of the incarnate Christ: His flesh is the new court where Gentiles enter, His soul the new holy place, His divinity the new holy of holies indwelt by the Father. This temple-Christology extends to ecclesiology: the Church as Christ's body inherits the temple typology, with baptism replacing circumcision as the gateway and the eucharist replacing the daily sacrifice as the perpetual offering.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). NICODEMUS the people is victor, a Pharisee and a member of the Sanhedrin. He is first noticed as visiting Jesus by night (John 3:1-21) for the purpose of learning more of his doctrines, which our Lord then unfolded to him, giving prominence to the necessity of being “born again.” He is next met with in the Sanhedrin (7:50-52), where he protested against the course they were taking in plotting against Christ. Once more he is mentioned as taking part in the preparation for the anointing and burial of the body of Christ (John 19:39). We hear nothing more of him. There can be little doubt that he became a true disciple.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Except a man be born again (anōthen), he cannot see the kingdom of God' is for Cyril the doctrinal axis of the entire Nicodemus pericope. The Greek 'anōthen' carries the double sense of 'again' (temporal) and 'from above' (spatial); Cyril preserves both: the new birth is at once a second temporal beginning AND a heavenly-origined event, not produced from human sources. This rebirth is necessary not as supplement to natural birth but as substitute for it on the order of grace: what natural birth gives (mortality, sin-inheritance, alienation from God) the rebirth replaces (incorruption, adoption, communion). The verse is the locus classicus for the Tewahedo doctrine of baptism as ontological renovation.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit' Cyril reads as the dominical institution of baptism: the two elements (water and Spirit) are inseparable, not sequential. Against the Messalians and other spiritualizing groups who would dispense with water and rely on a purely interior Spirit-experience, Cyril insists that the Spirit binds Himself to the water-sign in the Church's sacramental administration. The water is not merely symbolic accompaniment but the divinely-chosen visible vehicle of the Spirit's invisible regenerating act. This sacramental realism is the textual ground of the entire Tewahedo baptismal theology.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit' Cyril reads as Johannine confirmation of the doctrine of original sin: flesh begets only flesh, and the natural process of generation cannot transmit anything beyond the conditions of fallen creaturehood. Only the Spirit's begetting communicates spiritual life. Cyril is careful here to distinguish his reading from Manichaean dualism: 'flesh' is not evil per se but is wounded and unable to ascend to spiritual life without supernatural elevation. The Spirit's birth does not destroy the flesh but heals and elevates it — preparing for the bodily resurrection.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FALL OF MAN an expression probably borrowed from the Apocryphal Book of Wisdom, to express the fact of the revolt of our first parents from God, and the consequent sin and misery in which they and all their posterity were involved. The history of the Fall is recorded in Genesis 2 and 3. That history is to be literally interpreted. It records facts which underlie the whole system of revealed truth. It is referred to by our Lord and his apostles not only as being true, but as furnishing the ground of all God’s subsequent dispensations and dealings with the children of men. The record of Adam’s temptation and fall must be taken as a true historical account, if we are to understand the Bible at all as a revelation of God’s purpose of mercy. The effects of this first sin upon our first parents themselves were (1) “shame, a sense of degradation and pollution; (2) dread of the displeasure of God, or a sense of guilt, and the consequent desire to hide from his presence. These effects were unavoidable. They prove the loss not only of innocence but of original righteousness, and, with it, of the favour and fellowship of God. The state therefore to which Adam was reduced by his disobedience, so far as his subjective condition is concerned, was analogous to that of the fallen angels. He was entirely and absolutely ruined” (Hodge’s Theology). But the unbelief and disobedience of our first parents brought not only on themselves this misery and ruin, it entailed also the same sad consequences on all their descendants. (1.) The guilt, i.e., liability to punishment, of that sin comes by imputation upon all men, because all were represented by Adam in the covenant of works (q.v.). (See IMPUTATION.) (2.) Hence, also, all his descendants inherit a corrupt nature. In all by nature there is an inherent and prevailing tendency to sin. This universal depravity is taught by universal experience. All men sin as soon as they are capable of moral actions. The testimony of the Scriptures to the same effect is most abundant (Romans 1; 2; 3:1-19, etc.). (3.) This innate depravity is total: we are by nature “dead in trespasses and sins,” and must be “born again” before we can enter into the kingdom (John 3:7, etc.). (4.) Resulting from this “corruption of our whole nature” is our absolute moral inability to change our nature or to obey the law of God. Commenting on John 9:3, Ryle well remarks: “A deep and instructive principle lies in these words. They surely throw some light on that great question, the origin of evil. God has thought fit to allow evil to exist in order that he may have a platform for showing his mercy, grace, and compassion. If man had never fallen there would have been no opportunity of showing divine mercy. But by permitting evil, mysterious as it seems, God’s works of grace, mercy, and wisdom in saving sinners have been wonderfully manifested to all his creatures. The redeeming of the church of elect sinners is the means of ‘showing to principalities and powers the manifold wisdom of God’ (Ephesians 3:10). Without the Fall we should have known nothing of the Cross and the Gospel.” On the monuments of Egypt are found representations of a deity in human form, piercing with a spear the head of a serpent. This is regarded as an illustration of the wide dissemination of the tradition of the Fall. The story of the “golden age,” which gives place to the “iron age”, the age of purity and innocence, which is followed by a time when man becomes a prey to sin and misery, as represented in the mythology of Greece and Rome, has also been regarded as a tradition of the Fall.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

On 'The wind bloweth where it listeth' Cyril makes the most of the Greek pneuma's double sense (wind / spirit): the meteorological observation grounds the pneumatological doctrine. The Spirit's working in regeneration is sovereign (chooses its own subjects), audible-in-effects (the voice is heard), but invisible-in-cause (we cannot trace its origin or destination). Against Pelagian readings that would make human will the operative cause of regeneration, Cyril insists the Spirit's freedom is primary: regeneration is sovereign gift, even where it is mediated through baptism's prescribed channels. The Spirit who fills the prescribed channels is not bound by them.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'No man hath ascended up to heaven, but He that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven' is a verse Cyril uses to defend the *communicatio idiomatum* — the communication of attributes between Christ's divine and human natures in His one Person. The Son of man is 'in heaven' even while speaking to Nicodemus on earth: the divine attribute (omnipresence) is predicated of the human Person (Son of man) by virtue of the hypostatic union. Against Nestorian dilution (which would assign heavenly attributes only to the Logos-Person and earthly attributes only to the human-Person), Cyril here grounds the Miaphysite confession in Christ's own Johannine self-witness.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's typological self-reference — 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up' — Cyril develops with characteristic typological care. The bronze serpent was a likeness of the agent of death (the serpent) elevated as the means of healing; Christ on the cross is the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom 8:3) elevated as the means of salvation. The 'must' (dei) Cyril reads as expressing not external necessity (the schemes of His enemies) but the Father's eternal redemptive will to which the Son freely conforms. The Tewahedo Holy Week liturgy preserves this typological reading prominently.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

On the most-cited verse in the Gospel — 'For God so loved the world, that He gave His only-begotten Son' — Cyril builds the Athanasian-Cappadocian Trinitarian framework: the Father's love for the world is so radical that He gives not merely a creature or a prophet but His own consubstantial Son. The 'gave' (edōken) refers both to the Incarnation (the eternal Son's mission into flesh) and to the cross (the giving up to death) — the two are one redemptive movement. 'Only-begotten' (monogenēs) excludes any creaturely sonship: the Son's relation to the Father is unique, eternal, and inseparable. Cyril notes that 'the world' (kosmos) here means the whole of humanity, not the elect-narrowly — universal scope of love, particular efficacy of salvation through faith.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him' — for Cyril this Baptist's final discourse is also a Christological confession: the Son is the criterion of judgment. 'Hath' (echei, present tense) Cyril stresses: eternal life is not merely future promise but present possession of the believer through union with Christ. 'Abideth' (menei) for the wrath similarly denotes present condition, not future sentence: unbelief is itself the judgment, since refusing the Son cuts off from the only source of life. Cyril here grounds the realized-eschatology dimension of Johannine theology against any purely futurist readings.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JACOB’S WELL (John 4:5, 6). This is one of the few sites in Palestine about which there is no dispute. It was dug by Jacob, and hence its name, in the “parcel of ground” which he purchased from the sons of Hamor (Genesis 33:19). It still exists, but although after copious rains it contains a little water, it is now usually quite dry. It is at the entrance to the valley between Ebal and Gerizim, about 2 miles south-east of Shechem. It is about 9 feet in diameter and about 75 feet in depth, though in ancient times it was no doubt much deeper, probably twice as deep. The digging of such a well must have been a very laborious and costly undertaking. “Unfortunately, the well of Jacob has not escaped that misplaced religious veneration which cannot be satisfied with leaving the object of it as it is, but must build over it a shrine to protect and make it sacred. A series of buildings of various styles, and of different ages, have cumbered the ground, choked up the well, and disfigured the natural beauty and simplicity of the spot. At present the rubbish in the well has been cleared out; but there is still a domed structure over it, and you gaze down the shaft cut in the living rock and see at a depth of 70 feet the surface of the water glimmering with a pale blue light in the darkness, while you notice how the limestone blocks that form its curb have been worn smooth, or else furrowed by the ropes of centuries” (Hugh Macmillan). At the entrance of the enclosure round the well is planted in the ground one of the wooden poles that hold the telegraph wires between Jerusalem and Haifa.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's promise to the Samaritan woman — 'Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life' — Cyril reads pneumatologically: the water is the Holy Spirit Himself, given through Christ as His own gift to those who receive Him. The water's spring inside the believer (pēgē hydatos hallomenou) figures the Spirit's permanent indwelling, distinguished from the Old Covenant prophetic intermittent inspiration. 'Springing up' (hallomenou) carries the sense of leaping, dynamic ascent — the Spirit's indwelling is not static container but living source of theosis.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'The hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth' Cyril reads as the abrogation of the geographic-cultic restriction (Jerusalem temple / Mt. Gerizim) in favor of pneumatic-Christological worship. 'In spirit' is for Cyril 'in the Holy Spirit' (the worshipper's pneumatic transformation), and 'in truth' is 'in the Truth that is Christ' (Jn 14:6). True worship after the Incarnation is therefore Trinitarian: to the Father, in the Spirit, through the Truth-Son. This passage grounds the Tewahedo liturgical doctrine that the Anaphora's prayer is itself the Spirit's praying through the Church to the Father, mediated by the Christological elements.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'God is a Spirit' (pneuma ho theos) — Cyril reads this as ontological statement (the divine nature is spiritual, not material) and as missiological imperative (those who would worship a spiritual God must be spiritually transformed). Against the Anthropomorphites who attributed bodily form to God, Cyril insists the verse settles the question: God has no parts, no extension, no spatial location. Yet against any Hellenizing collapse of God into pure abstraction, Cyril preserves the personal-relational character: the Spirit-God is the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit — three Persons in one spiritual essence. Worship 'in spirit and in truth' is therefore the only worship corresponding to God's actual mode of being.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'My meat is to do the will of Him that sent me, and to finish His work' Cyril reads as Christ's self-disclosure of the perfect harmony between His human will and the Father's eternal will. Against the Apollinarian denial of Christ's human soul (or against any reading that would make Christ's will merely divine), Cyril here recognizes that Christ has a genuinely human will, but it is so perfectly conformed to the Father's will that 'doing the Father's will' becomes His characteristic sustenance — what physical food is to bodily life, the doing of the divine will is to Christ's incarnate human life. This is the seed of the dyothelite-anticipation that becomes explicit in later Greek theology, though Cyril himself does not yet use those terms.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

The Samaritans' climactic confession — 'This is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world' (ho sōtēr tou kosmou) — Cyril emphasizes as the proleptic Gentile recognition of Christ's universal salvific scope. The Samaritans, themselves marginal to Jewish covenant identity, become the prototype for the Gentile inclusion that will mark the post-Pentecost Church. 'Saviour of the world' is for Cyril a title both universal (Christ saves the world, not merely a portion) and particular (each person is saved as individual within that universal scope). The Tewahedo Synaxarium honors Photine (the traditional name of the Samaritan woman) on the 26th of Hidar — her witness to her village becomes the first apostolic missionary act recorded in John.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's command to the paralytic — 'Rise, take up thy bed, and walk' — Cyril reads as the threefold pattern of every healing the Word performs in the soul: resurrection from spiritual death (rise), taking up the burden of one's former weakness as instrument rather than master (take up thy bed), and active progress in the new life (walk). The thirty-eight years of paralysis Cyril typologically links with the thirty-eight years of Israel's wilderness wandering (Deut 2:14) — both the individual and the people are healed by direct sovereign address, not by mediating ceremony or stirred-pool waiting. The Sabbath setting prepares Cyril's larger argument: Christ exercises the Father's authority over the Sabbath because He is consubstantial with the Father.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'My Father worketh hitherto, and I work' (heōs arti) — Cyril reads as one of the most decisive anti-Arian sayings in the Gospel. The Sabbath rest of Gen 2:2 did not mean God ceased operating (providence is unbroken); Christ here claims the same uninterrupted operative power that belongs to the Father. The 'and I' (kagō) refuses any subordination: the Son's working is co-equal, co-eternal, co-extensive with the Father's. The Jews' immediate reaction (5:18: they sought to kill Him for 'making Himself equal with God') confirms they understood the claim correctly. Cyril uses this verse against the Eusebian semi-Arians of his own day who would dilute the Son's operative parity with the Father.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

The Jews' interpretation — that Christ was 'making Himself equal with God' (ison heauton poiōn tō Theō) — Cyril takes as inspired witness, not hostile misreading. Even Christ's opponents recognized that calling God 'my Father' (idion Patera) in this manner was a claim to consubstantial equality, not adoptive sonship. Cyril notes the Greek 'idion' (own/proper) carries the sense of natural-not-merely-adoptive: the Son's relation to the Father differs in kind, not just degree, from any creature's. This verse is one of Cyril's strongest scriptural anchors against Arian and Eunomian readings — even the unbelieving witnesses confirm the orthodox reading.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'The Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He seeth the Father do' Cyril reads with extreme care against Arian misreading. The 'can do nothing of Himself' is NOT a statement of weakness or subordination but of perfect Trinitarian harmony: the Son's operations are inseparable from the Father's because of their consubstantial unity. The 'seeing' is not perceptual observation (as if the Son had to watch what the Father did) but eternal mutual indwelling of co-equal Persons. 'What things soever He doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise' (homoiōs) Cyril stresses: not subordinately, not differently, but identically — every divine work belongs to all three Persons indivisibly.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'As the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth them; even so the Son quickeneth whom He will' — Cyril takes the absolute power of the eschatological resurrection as the supreme proof of consubstantiality. To raise the dead is a work exclusively divine; for the Son to share this power without limit means He shares the divine nature. 'Whom He will' (hous thelei) Cyril emphasizes: not a delegated authority to be exercised within constraints, but sovereign personal choice — the same will that the Father exercises. The verse also establishes the personalist character of resurrection: Christ raises individuals by His sovereign decision, not as automatic effect of cosmic process.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'The Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son' Cyril reads as the eschatological consummation of the Father-Son economy: the Father's universal judgment is exercised through the incarnate Son, who because of His shared human nature is uniquely fit to judge humanity. The 'committed' (dedōken) Cyril carefully distinguishes from any subordinationist reading: this is not a delegation of authority the Father lacks the will to exercise directly, but the manifestation of the eternal Trinitarian order — every operation 'from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit' (Cyril's standard formula). This verse grounds Cyril's later argument (in the Twelve Anathemas) that the man-God Christ, not a separate human judge, presides at the Last Day.

↩ ◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos III.16 (c. 350 AD)

'That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him' — Athanasius marks hina pantes timōsi ton Huion kathōs timōsi ton Patera (that all should honor the Son EVEN AS they honor the Father) as the HOMOTĪMION (equal-honor) prooftext. Equal-honor is owed-by-creatures only to one equal-in-nature (homoousios) with the Father; therefore the kathōs (EVEN AS, in-the-same-manner-as) directly entails homoousion. Any reduction of the Son to creature-status would make this equal-honor idolatrous; the Word's-own-claim therefore-positively-requires divine-essence. Pairs with Phil 2:10 (every-knee-shall-bow at-the-name-of-Jesus) as the canonical equal-divine-worship pair.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'He that heareth my word, and believeth on Him that sent me, HATH everlasting life' Cyril reads as one of the strongest realized-eschatology pins in the Gospel: eternal life is not merely promised for the future but present possession of the believer through faith. 'Is passed from death unto life' (metabebēken — perfect tense, completed action with continuing result) confirms the present reality: the believer has ALREADY transitioned from the death-realm to the life-realm. This is not denial of future bodily resurrection (which Cyril affirms strongly) but recognition that the spiritual-ontological transition has already occurred for those united to Christ by faith. The verse grounds Cyril's sacramental realism: baptism enacts what faith receives.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'As the Father hath life in Himself, so hath He given to the Son to have life in Himself' is for Cyril a critical text for the Son's natural-not-derived divinity. The 'given' (edōken) is not temporal grant (as if the Son did not always possess what He now has) but eternal communication of essence — the Father eternally communicates to the Son the same divine life He has from Himself. To 'have life in Himself' (echein zōēn en heautō) is the divine attribute par excellence: not life received from elsewhere, but life as one's own essence. The Father has it without source; the Son has it from the Father, yet equally and eternally. This is Cyril's most precise statement of the Cappadocian-Athanasian doctrine of eternal generation.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me' Cyril takes as the dominical hermeneutical principle: the Hebrew Scriptures are properly read only when read Christologically. Against Marcion's rejection of the Old Testament and against the Jewish rejection of its messianic-Christological reading, Cyril positions the verse as Christ's own self-witness: He IS the proper subject of the Scriptures. 'Ye think' (dokeite) is gentle correction: searching the Scriptures for eternal life apart from recognizing Christ in them is futile — the life they testify to is the life He brings. This verse grounds the entire Alexandrian typological hermeneutic.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me' Cyril reads as Christ's authoritative claim to be the proper object of every Mosaic prophecy. The verse establishes the principle that Moses and Christ stand in continuity, not discontinuity: rejection of Christ is rejection of Moses (and conversely, true reception of Moses leads to Christ). Cyril uses this verse against any Manichaean or Marcionite reading that would oppose the Testaments; he also uses it against any Jewish reading that would treat Mosaic obedience as sufficient apart from Christological reception. The Tewahedo Pentateuch readings in the Mäṣḥafä Qǝddase preserve this Cyrilline unity by always pairing Torah readings with their Christological NT fulfillment.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). TIBERIAS a city, the modern Tubarich, on the western shore of the Sea of Tiberias. It is said to have been founded by Herod Antipas (A.D. 16), on the site of the ruins of an older city called Rakkath, and to have been thus named by him after the Emperor Tiberius. It is mentioned only three times in the history of our Lord (John 6:1,23; 21:1). In 1837 about one-half of the inhabitants perished by an earthquake. The population of the city is now about six thousand, nearly the one-half being Jews. “We do not read that our Lord ever entered this city. The reason of this is probably to be found in the fact that it was practically a heathen city, though standing upon Jewish soil. Herod, its founder, had brought together the arts of Greece, the idolatry of Rome, and the gross lewdness of Asia. There were in it a theatre for the performance of comedies, a forum, a stadium, a palace roofed with gold in imitation of those in Italy, statues of the Roman gods, and busts of the deified emperors. He who was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel might well hold himself aloof from such scenes as these” (Manning’s Those Holy Fields). After the fall of Jerusalem (A.D. 70), Tiberias became one of the chief residences of the Jews in Palestine. It was for more than three hundred years their metropolis. From about A.D. 150 the Sanhedrin settled here, and established rabbinical schools, which rose to great celebrity. Here the Jerusalem (or Palestinian) Talmud was compiled about the beginning of the fifth century. To this same rabbinical school also we are indebted for the Masora, a “body of traditions which transmitted the readings of the Hebrew text of the Old Testament, and preserved, by means of the vowel-system, the pronunciation of the Hebrew.” In its original form, and in all manuscripts, the Hebrew is written without vowels; hence, when it ceased to be a spoken language, the importance of knowing what vowels to insert between the consonants. This is supplied by the Masora, and hence these vowels are called the “Masoretic vowel-points.”

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

On the multiplication of loaves Cyril notes the deliberate eucharistic prefiguration: Christ TOOK the loaves, gave THANKS (eucharistēsas), and distributed. The four-fold pattern (take / bless / break / give) that becomes the Mass Cyril sees inaugurated here — the feeding of the five thousand is the sign that points to the institution at the Last Supper and the perpetual continuation in the Anaphora. The crowd's hunger Cyril takes typologically: humanity hungers for the bread of eternal life which only Christ can give; physical hunger is the symptom of the deeper spiritual hunger. The Tewahedo Anaphora's preparation prayers preserve this typological reading explicitly.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life' Cyril reads as Christ's hermeneutic for understanding the previous miracle: the loaves were sign, not substance — the substance is the eucharistic bread that gives eternal life. 'Which the Son of man shall give unto you' (dōsei — future tense) Cyril emphasizes: pointing forward to the institution of the eucharist, not to repeat-feedings of physical bread. 'For him hath God the Father sealed' Cyril reads as the Spirit's anointing that makes Christ's human nature the perpetual source of the bread of life — the seal of the Spirit on the incarnate Son is what makes the eucharistic gift possible.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I am the bread of life' (egō eimi ho artos tēs zōēs) — the first of Christ's great 'I AM' sayings in John — Cyril reads as both ontological self-disclosure and sacramental promise. The 'I am' echoes the divine name (Ex 3:14: ego eimi ho ōn); the 'bread of life' identifies the specific mode of Christ's gift to His Church. 'He that cometh to me shall never hunger, and he that believeth on me shall never thirst' Cyril takes as the perfect parallel between coming-to-Christ (sacramentally: through baptism into His body) and believing-on-Him (fiducially: through saving faith) — neither alone, but both together produce the perpetual satisfaction of spiritual hunger and thirst.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of Him that sent me' Cyril reads against any reading that would set the Son's will in opposition to the Father's. The 'not mine own' (ouch hina poiō) does not deny that the Son HAS a will (Apollinarian denial), nor does it imply imperfect alignment requiring submission. Rather, Cyril notes the Son's INCARNATE human will is now in question: as man, the Son receives the Father's will and acts upon it; as God, His will is identical with the Father's by nature. This is one of Cyril's earliest articulations of what later dyothelite theology would systematize: two wills (divine + human) in one Person, perfectly aligned.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him' Cyril reads as the Johannine doctrine of prevenient grace. The Father's 'drawing' (helkysē) is the operative work of grace that precedes and enables human response to Christ; without it, no one comes. Cyril is careful here against Pelagian readings: the verse strictly excludes natural human capacity to come to Christ apart from divine initiative. Yet the 'drawing' is not coercive — Cyril (following the classic patristic distinction) reads it as the Father's drawing through the Spirit's inward attraction, which the human will may still resist (against later Augustinian readings that would make it irresistible). This passage grounds the Eastern Christian doctrine of synergism: grace initiates, the will cooperates.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world' is for Cyril the central eucharistic-Christological text in the entire Gospel. The bread Christ gives IS His own flesh — the personal Word's true flesh, not a metaphor or symbol, but the incarnate body offered on the cross and now communicated through the eucharist. 'For the life of the world' confirms the universal scope of the offering — not for the elect alone, not for the Jews alone, but for the kosmos. Cyril uses this verse as the textual foundation for his doctrine of eucharistic realism that becomes determinative for all subsequent Greek and Oriental Orthodox theology.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink His blood, ye have no life in you' Cyril takes with full sacramental seriousness: this is not metaphor but ontological condition. The eucharistic eating-and-drinking is the necessary means by which the life of the incarnate Word is communicated to the believer's body and soul. Against any spiritualizing reading that would dissolve the verse into mere faith-receptive metaphor, Cyril insists the verse means what it says: the actual flesh and blood of Christ, sacramentally present, must be actually received. 'Ye have no life in you' (ouk echete zōēn en heautois) is the privative consequence of refusing the eucharistic gift. This is the locus classicus of Cyril's eucharistic theology that the Tewahedo Anaphora preserves verbatim.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day' Cyril reads as the eucharistic guarantee of bodily resurrection. The flesh of Christ communicated to the believer's body becomes the seed of the resurrection body — Cyril's standard formula is that the eucharist is the 'medicine of immortality' (pharmakon athanasias, from Ignatius). The 'I will raise him up' is Christ's personal promise tied to the eucharistic reception: the body that has received the Body of Christ has within it the seed of eschatological transformation. This verse anchors Cyril's distinctive contribution to eucharistic theology: the sacrament does not merely commemorate or symbolize, it actually communicates the resurrection life.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'For my flesh is meat indeed (alēthōs), and my blood is drink indeed' Cyril takes as decisive against any reading that would weaken eucharistic realism. The Greek 'alēthōs' means 'truly / really / actually' — Christ here explicitly disqualifies any metaphorical or symbolic interpretation of His preceding words. Against the gnostics of his own era and against any anticipatory spiritualizing readings, Cyril insists: TRULY flesh, REALLY blood — the eucharistic gift IS what it appears to be on the level of substance, even while remaining bread and wine to the senses. This is Cyril's clearest articulation of what later Western scholasticism would call the doctrine of real presence (without scholastic categories of substance/accidents).

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'It is the Spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing' Cyril famously handles with great care against capernaitic misreadings that would take 'eating the flesh' as cannibalistic physical consumption. The 'flesh' that profiteth nothing is fleshly-mode-of-understanding, not the actual flesh of Christ (which gives life). The verse means: receiving the eucharist with merely carnal comprehension — as if Christ's body were divided physically among communicants like ordinary food — is profitless. Only Spirit-quickened reception receives the gift as it truly is. This is Cyril's careful pneumatological qualification of his strong eucharistic realism: the realism is true, but its appropriation is spiritual, not crudely physical.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'My doctrine is not mine, but His that sent me' Cyril carefully defends against Arian misreading. The 'not mine' does NOT deny the Son's possession of the doctrine but identifies its source: the Son's teaching is not innovative or independent but is the eternal teaching of the Father, possessed by the Son by nature (consubstantial communication of all divine attributes including wisdom-teaching). Cyril notes the parallel to 5:30: 'I can of mine own self do nothing' — both texts speak of perfect Trinitarian harmony, not of any inferiority in the Son. The Son's teaching IS the Father's teaching because the Son IS the eternal Word who speaks the Father's mind.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (428). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'If any man will do His will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God' Cyril takes as the dominical statement of moral epistemology: knowledge of divine truth is conditioned on willingness to obey. Against any purely intellectual approach to theological knowledge (which would make speculation independent of holiness), Cyril here grounds the patristic axiom: theology requires askesis. The 'will to do His will' (thelē to thelēma autou poiein) Cyril emphasizes as primary disposition; the cognitive recognition follows on it. This verse becomes the textual root of the entire Eastern Orthodox tradition that knowledge of God presupposes purification of the nous through ascetic practice.
