↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the parable of the lost coin — 'Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?' (Lk 15:8) — Cyril reads the maternal-housekeeping-image as the canonical Lukan anchor of a doctrine that complements the shepherd-image (Lk 15:4) and the father-image (Lk 15:11): God seeks the lost in three iconic ways — shepherd seeking on the hills, woman seeking in the house, father waiting at the door. The triple-image is Trinitarian-iconic-pedagogy. Tewahedo Trinitarian-iconography cites Lk 15:4-32 as the canonical Lukan iconographic triple-pattern of the Father-Son-Spirit's-shared-search-for-the-lost.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the parable's opening 'A certain man had two sons' (Lk 15:11), Cyril reads the two-sons frame as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the parable's THIRD pivot (after shepherd + housekeeper) gives the Father his speaking-part: the father whose first speech is the silent embrace at 15:20, whose second speech is the celebration-command, whose third is the explanation to the elder brother. The full-pericope (Lk 15:11-32) is Christ's most-extended-character-development parable; the father's character is most-fully-disclosed. Tewahedo pastoral theology cites Lk 15:11-32 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the Father's threefold-speech-of-mercy — the priest who absolves speaks as the father in the parable speaks.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CITIZENSHIP the rights and privileges of a citizen in distinction from a foreigner (Luke 15:15; 19:14; Acts 21:39). Under the Mosaic law non-Israelites, with the exception of the Moabites and the Ammonites and others mentioned in Deuteronomy 23:1-3, were admitted to the general privileges of citizenship among the Jews (Exodus 12:19; Leviticus 24:22; Numbers 15:15; 35:15; Deuteronomy 10:18; 14:29; 16:10, 14). The right of citizenship under the Roman government was granted by the emperor to individuals, and sometimes to provinces, as a favour or as a recompense for services rendered to the state, or for a sum of money (Acts 22:28). This “freedom” secured privileges equal to those enjoyed by natives of Rome. Among the most notable of these was the provision that a man could not be bound or imprisoned without a formal trial (Acts 22:25, 26), or scourged (16:37). All Roman citizens had the right of appeal to Caesar (25:11).

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

'When he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him' — Cyril treats the Father's running as the canonical signature of the Lukan parable: the divine compassion does not wait for the sinner to arrive but goes out to meet him while he is still far. The first robe, the ring, and the shoes are the baptismal restoration of dignity. Tewahedo penitential theology cites Lk 15:20-22 as the principal canonical anchor of God-runs-to-meet-the-returning-sinner imagery.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the father's final words to the elder brother 'It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found' (Lk 15:32), Cyril reads the doubled-formula (dead-and-alive + lost-and-found) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of conversion-as-resurrection: the prodigal's return is not merely moral-improvement but a passage from death to life. The same doubled-formula echoes Christian baptism (Rom 6:4 — dead with Christ, alive in Christ). Tewahedo baptismal-and-penance theology cites Lk 15:32 + Rom 6:4 as the canonical doubled-witness that every conversion is a participation in the death-and-resurrection of Christ; the Tewahedo penance-rite preserves the alive-again grammar in its absolution formula.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the master's commendation of the unjust steward — 'the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely' (Lk 16:8) — Cyril reads the lord-commended-the-unjust paradox as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that prudent-shrewdness in temporal matters should be matched by prudent-shrewdness in eternal matters: the steward is praised not for his dishonesty but for his foresight in securing his future. Tewahedo stewardship theology cites Lk 16:8 + Lk 16:9 ('make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness') as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of strategic-almsgiving — the prudent Christian uses temporal wealth to build eternal friendships (the recipients of the alms welcome the giver into eternal habitations).

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'No servant can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon' (Lk 16:13), Cyril reads the impossibility-formula (ou dynasthe — 'ye CANNOT') as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the metaphysical incompatibility of God and mammon as objects-of-ultimate-loyalty: the disjunction is not pastoral counsel but ontological fact. Cyril notes the personification of mammon (treated as a rival lord) anticipates later patristic identifications of mammon-greed as a demonic principality. Tewahedo asceticism cites Lk 16:13 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that monastic poverty is the only consistent answer to the impossibility-formula — the bahǝtawi physically forecloses the option of serving mammon.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the parable's opening 'There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day' (Lk 16:19), Cyril reads the unnamed-rich-man + named-Lazarus contrast as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the reversal-of-recognition: the rich man (anonymous in the parable, anonymous in heaven) has his fine-linen reversed to torment; the poor man Lazarus (named, known to God) has his sores reversed to glory. The parable is Christ's most-vivid teaching on the post-mortem intermediate state — the doctrine elaborated at 16:23 seed. Tewahedo intermediate-state theology cites Lk 16:19 + Lk 16:23 + Lk 23:43 (good thief) as the canonical Lukan triple-witness for the conscious-intermediate-state of departed souls.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ABRAHAM’S BOSOM (Luke 16:22,23) refers to the custom of reclining on couches at table, which was prevalent among the Jews, an arrangement which brought the head of one person almost into the bosom of the one who sat or reclined above him. To “be in Abraham’s bosom” thus meant to enjoy happiness and rest (Matthew 8:11; Luke 16:23) at the banquet in Paradise. (See BANQUET; MEALS.)

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

Cyril reads the Rich-Man-and-Lazarus narrative as canonically settling several intermediate-state questions: that there is consciousness after death; that the just are gathered to a place of refreshment ('Abraham's bosom'); that the unjust suffer torment in conscious recognition; that the chasm fixed between the two is uncrossable; that Moses and the Prophets are sufficient witnesses to deter the living. Tewahedo eschatology draws on Lk 16:19-31 as the principal canonical Lukan anchor of the intermediate-state doctrine.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the rich man's plea + Abraham's answer 'If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead' (Lk 16:31), Cyril reads Abraham's verdict as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the sufficiency-of-Scripture for salvation: even resurrection-witness will not persuade those who have hardened against the canonical word. The verse becomes load-bearing in the Lukan-Acts trajectory: the post-resurrection apostolic preaching cites the OT Scriptures as the basis of belief (Acts 17:11 — Bereans searched the Scriptures). Tewahedo bibliology cites Lk 16:31 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the canonical Scriptures are sufficient for salvation; private revelations and apparitions are accountable to that canonical word.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the apostles' petition 'Lord, increase our faith' (Lk 17:5), Cyril reads the prosthes-hēmin-pistin (add-to-us-faith) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that faith is a gift to be asked for, not a quality to be produced: the apostles do not say 'we will work harder' but 'Lord, give us more'. Christ's mustard-seed answer (Lk 17:6) does not rebuke the request but redirects it — faith's POWER is not in its quantity but in its OBJECT (God's omnipotence). Tewahedo faith-formation cites Lk 17:5 + Lk 17:6 as the canonical doubled-Lukan-witness that faith is request-receivable from God (not striven-produced by self) and small-but-real-faith is sufficient if its object is the true God.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SYCAMINE TREE mentioned only in Luke 17:6. It is rendered by Luther “mulberry tree” (q.v.), which is most probably the correct rendering. It is found of two species, the black mulberry (Morus nigra) and the white mulberry (Mourea), which are common in Palestine. The silk-worm feeds on their leaves. The rearing of them is one of the chief industries of the peasantry of Lebanon and of other parts of the land. It is of the order of the fig-tree. Some contend, however, that this name denotes the sycamore-fig of Luke 19:4.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do' (Lk 17:10), Cyril reads the unprofitable-servants-formula as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of grace-against-merit: even maximal Christian-virtuous-action puts the disciple no further than baseline-duty; salvation is never owed to the disciple. The Greek achreioi (unprofitable, but also 'without-superfluous-claim') captures the disposition of the just-debtor with no surplus. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 17:10 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the monk's perpetual-humility-formula — 'I am an unprofitable servant' is recited in the daily-office.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

Only the Samaritan among the ten cleansed lepers returns to give thanks at Christ's feet, and Cyril reads the verse as the canonical Lukan anchor of the eucharistic posture: the cleansed turn back to the cleanser in thanksgiving (eucharistia). The nine who do not return are not cured of the deeper leprosy of ingratitude. Tewahedo Anaphora preserves the Cyrillian reading: the proper response to divine cleansing is the return-to-the-altar with thanks.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'the kingdom of God is within you' (Lk 17:21 — entos hymōn estin), Cyril reads the entos-hymōn (within-you or among-you) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the present-immanent-kingdom: in Christ's person and ministry, the kingdom has already arrived among the questioners — the Pharisees see-but-do-not-recognize it. Cyril allows both readings (within = interior reign of God in the believer; among = Christ-the-kingdom-present-among). The Greek is deliberately ambiguous. Tewahedo theology of the kingdom cites Lk 17:21 + Mk 1:15 ('the kingdom of God is at hand') as the canonical doubled-witness for the already-present (Christological) and the still-coming (eschatological) dimensions of the kingdom.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's terse warning 'Remember Lot's wife' (Lk 17:32), Cyril reads the imperative-of-memory (mnēmoneuete) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that disobedient-looking-back is a paradigmatic-fatal-sin: Lot's wife (Gen 19:26) is preserved in canonical-memory not as a personal-name but as a warning-icon. The eschatological context (Lk 17:31 — that day, the rooftop) makes the warning explicit: when the kingdom comes, no looking-back. Tewahedo eschatological-asceticism cites Lk 17:32 + Lk 9:62 (plough-no-looking-back) as the canonical doubled-Lukan-witness for the irreversibility-of-disciple-orientation — both verses use the same forward-orientation grammar.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Luke's editorial introduction to the unjust-judge parable — 'he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint' (Lk 18:1) — Cyril reads the dei-pantote-proseuchesthai (it-is-necessary-always-to-pray) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of ceaseless-prayer (later codified by Paul at 1 Th 5:17 — 'pray without ceasing'). The grammatical necessity (dei) puts ceaseless-prayer on the same canonical level as 'must-be-baptized' and 'must-suffer'. Tewahedo monastic-prayer-discipline cites Lk 18:1 + 1 Th 5:17 as the canonical doubled-witness for the seven-fold daily office (Mäshafä Sǝʾatat) — seven daily prayer-points are the canonical operationalization of 'always pray, never faint'.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the Pharisee's self-praising prayer 'God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are' (Lk 18:11), Cyril reads the Pharisee's-prayer as the canonical Lukan anti-model: addressed-to-God-in-form but self-praising-in-content. The prepositional pros-heauton (with-himself / to-himself — preferred reading) makes the Pharisee's prayer self-directed even in posture. Tewahedo confessor's-prayer-formation cites Lk 18:11 + Lk 18:13 (the Publican's prayer — seed γ.4.3) as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness of the two-prayer-patterns: the wrong one (Pharisee, self-praise) and the right one (Publican, 'God be merciful to me a sinner' — the Jesus-Prayer of Tewahedo monastic-spirituality).

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

The publican standing afar off, smiting on his breast, saying 'God be merciful to me a sinner' — Cyril treats this prayer as the canonical Lukan form of the Jesus-prayer: short, exact, self-acknowledging, mercy-petitioning. The publican goes down to his house justified, not the Pharisee. Tewahedo monastic prayer tradition preserves the publican's prayer as the canonical seed of the continual prayer of the heart.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's command 'Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God' (Lk 18:16), Cyril reads the doubled-imperative (suffer-them + forbid-them-not) as the canonical Lukan anchor of paedo-receptivity and (in the wider patristic tradition) infant-baptism: children are not deferred until adult-comprehension but received-now into the kingdom. The kingdom belongs not to children alone but to those characterized by child-like receptivity (Lk 18:17). Tewahedo baptismal theology — practising infant-baptism (often on the 40th day for boys, 80th day for girls per Lev 12 + Lk 2:22-24) — cites Lk 18:16 as the canonical Lukan-NT anchor for the practice.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's command to the rich young ruler 'Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me' (Lk 18:22), Cyril reads the sell-all + follow-me as the canonical Lukan anchor of the monastic-vocation specifically (not universal divestment for every Christian — Cyril is careful here): some are called to total-divestment as a particular vocation, and the rich-young-ruler is identified as such a call-and-refusal narrative. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 18:22 + Acts 4:34-35 (early-Jerusalem communal-divestment) as the canonical doubled-witness for the monastic vocation; the cenobitic-Tewahedo monasteries preserve the apostolic-divestment pattern.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

The blind beggar at Jericho — 'Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me' — gives, for Cyril, the canonical short-form messianic address. The blind man sees by faith what the seeing crowd does not see: the Davidic sonship of the passing Christ. Tewahedo invocation of the Jesus-prayer preserves the blind-beggar address as one of its earliest canonical forms.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ZACCHAEUS pure, a superintendant of customs; a chief tax-gather (publicanus) at Jericho (Luke 19:1-10). “The collection of customs at Jericho, which at this time produced and exported a considerable quantity of balsam, was undoubtedly an important post, and would account for Zacchaeus being a rich man.” Being short of stature, he hastened on before the multitude who were thronging about Christ as he passed through Jericho on his way to Jerusalem, and climbed up a sycamore tree that he might be able to see him. When our Lord reached the spot he looked up to the publican among the branches, and addressing him by name, told him to make haste and come down, as he intended that day to abide at his house. This led to the remarkable interview recorded by the evangelist, and to the striking parable of the ten pounds (Luke 19:12-27). At Er-riha (Jericho) there is a large, venerable looking square tower, which goes by the traditional name of the House of Zacchaeus.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Judea, Modern.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: HOSPITALITY, JERICHO, JESUS, THE CHRIST, JESUS, THE CHRIST, PUBLICANS.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PUBLICAN one who farmed the taxes (e.g., Zacchaeus, Luke 19:2) to be levied from a town or district, and thus undertook to pay to the supreme government a certain amount. In order to collect the taxes, the publicans employed subordinates (5:27; 15:1; 18:10), who, for their own ends, were often guilty of extortion and peculation. In New Testament times these taxes were paid to the Romans, and hence were regarded by the Jews as a very heavy burden, and hence also the collectors of taxes, who were frequently Jews, were hated, and were usually spoken of in very opprobrious terms. Jesus was accused of being a “friend of publicans and sinners” (Luke 7:34).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SYCAMORE more properly sycomore (Hebrews shikmoth and shikmim, Gr. sycomoros), a tree which in its general character resembles the fig-tree, while its leaves resemble those of the mulberry; hence it is called the fig-mulberry (Ficus sycomorus). At Jericho, Zacchaeus climbed a sycomore-tree to see Jesus as he passed by (Luke 19:4). This tree was easily destroyed by frost (Psalm 78:47), and therefore it is found mostly in the “vale” (1 Kings 10:27; 2 Chronicles 1:15: in both passages the R.V. has properly “lowland”), i.e., the “low country,” the shephelah, where the climate is mild. Amos (7:14) refers to its fruit, which is of an inferior character; so also probably Jeremiah (24:2). It is to be distinguished from our sycamore (the Acer pseudo-platanus), which is a species of maple often called a plane-tree.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's call to Zacchaeus 'make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house' (Lk 19:5), Cyril reads the dei-me (it-is-necessary-for-me) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's seeking-grace: the dominical 'I must lodge with thee' is a divine-imperative, not a guest's-request. Christ initiates the encounter; Zacchaeus's tree-climbing met halfway by Christ's calling-down. Tewahedo evangelism-theology cites Lk 19:5 + Lk 19:10 (Son of Man come to seek-and-save) as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness of the doctrine that Christ initiates the salvation-encounter; the priestly-pastor follows the dominical-pattern of seeking-the-Zacchaeuses.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

'This day is salvation come to this house' — Cyril reads the Zacchaeus pericope as the canonical Lukan diptych to Lk 15: in Lk 15 the lost son returns to the father; in Lk 19 the lost son is sought-and-found by the Father. The Son of Man came TO SEEK AND TO SAVE — the seeking is the divine initiative. Tewahedo missiology cites Lk 19:10 alongside Lk 15:20 as the canonical seeking-and-running diptych.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's mission-statement at the Zacchaeus episode 'For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost' (Lk 19:10), Cyril reads the doubled-mission (seek + save) as the canonical Lukan summary-statement of the Incarnation's purpose: the Son of Man's earthly trajectory (already-emphasized at Lk 5:32 — come to call sinners) reaches its compact-definitive expression here. The verse becomes load-bearing for the patristic doctrine of the missio Dei — God's outgoing mission preceding any human response. Tewahedo missionary theology cites Lk 19:10 + Lk 5:32 as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness of the doctrine that Christian mission participates in the dominical-search-and-rescue mission; the Tewahedo apostolic-outreach to the Beta-Israel and surrounding peoples is the appropriation of this canonical pattern.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the triumphal-entry cry 'Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest' (Lk 19:38), Cyril reads the Lukan-distinctive 'peace in heaven' (where the Synoptic parallels say 'Hosanna in the highest') as the canonical Lukan anchor of the cosmic-reconciliation announcement: heaven-and-earth peace is the explicit content of Christ's triumphal-entry. The phrase echoes the angelic Christmas-hymn (Lk 2:14 — peace-on-earth) and now reverses: peace-on-earth then, peace-in-heaven now. Tewahedo Hosanna-procession (Hosanna feast — the Sunday before Pascha) cites Lk 19:38 alongside Lk 2:14 as the canonical Lukan-doubled-witness of the peace-of-the-incarnation completed at the Cross.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

Christ's weeping over Jerusalem is for Cyril the canonical disclosure of the Lord's mercy precisely toward the city about to reject him. The tears do not soften the prophetic announcement of the city's destruction; they intensify it as the announcement of a real and grievous loss. Cyril rejects every reading that would treat the tears as mere stagecraft. Tewahedo Holy-Week lectionary preserves Lk 19:41-44 as the Palm-Sunday-eve reading of the Lord's lament.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's cleansing of the Temple — 'It is written, My house is the house of prayer: but ye have made it a den of thieves' (Lk 19:46) — Cyril reads the citation of Isa 56:7 + Jer 7:11 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the consecrated-place is by-definition the house-of-prayer; commerce within the precinct DEFILES the consecration. Christ's action is canonical-prophetic, not anti-Temple in principle (Christ continues to teach there daily, Lk 19:47). Tewahedo church-discipline cites Lk 19:46 + Is 56:7 + Jer 7:11 as the canonical triple-witness that the church-building is by definition the house-of-prayer; commercial use of the precinct (vending, money-changing) is excluded by canonical prophet-and-dominical authority.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the Temple-elders' challenge 'by what authority doest thou these things?' (Lk 20:1-2), Cyril reads the authority-question as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christ's authority is self-authenticating, not derived from human institutions: the Lord refuses to license his actions to the question-form because to do so would already concede that authority is delegable by the Sanhedrin. Christ's counter-question about John's baptism (Lk 20:4) traps the elders in their own institutional logic. Tewahedo ecclesial theology cites Lk 20:1-8 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the Church's authority traces to Christ directly, not through Imperial-Sanhedrin-style human delegation.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the parable of the wicked husbandmen (Lk 20:9-16), Cyril reads the vineyard-tenants who reject the servants and finally kill the heir as the canonical Lukan anchor of the salvation-history-as-progressive-rejection: prophets sent, prophets killed; finally the Son sent, the Son killed; the vineyard given to others (Gentiles + Tewahedo). The 'heir' language is Christological: Christ's death is the prophetic-final rejection that opens the vineyard to the wider mission. Tewahedo missionary-theology cites Lk 20:9-16 + Mt 21:43 ('the kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof') as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the Gentile-Ethiopian inclusion in the vineyard is the consequence of the canonical-prophetic rejection of Christ at Calvary.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's citation 'The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner' (Lk 20:17, citing Ps 118:22), Cyril reads the stone-rejected-yet-cornerstone as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the Christological-rejection-reversal: Christ is the rejected stone (by the Jerusalem builders) who becomes the foundation-cornerstone of the New-Covenant building (apostolic + Gentile-inclusion). The citation chain runs Ps 118:22 → Lk 20:17 → Acts 4:11 (Peter's apostolic preaching) → 1 Pet 2:6-8 (foundation theology). Tewahedo ecclesiology cites this canonical chain as the foundation of the doctrine that the Tewahedo Church is built on Christ-the-Cornerstone, not on the rejecting Jerusalem-builders' approval.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

'Render therefore unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's, and unto God the things which be God's' — Cyril treats the saying as the canonical two-spheres principle: civic duty is real but subordinate, and never displaces the duty to God. The denarius carries Caesar's image; the soul carries God's. The implicit argument is that the soul is rendered to God by being conformed to his image. Tewahedo political theology cites Lk 20:25 as the canonical two-kingdoms anchor.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the Sadducees' resurrection-denying scenario (the woman-with-seven-husbands at Lk 20:27-33), Cyril reads the Sadducees' rejection-of-resurrection as the canonical anti-pattern: those who deny the resurrection prove they neither know the Scriptures (the basis of resurrection-hope) nor the power of God (the agent of resurrection). The Sadducees' literalistic-marriage scenario fundamentally misunderstands that resurrection-life is transformed-life, not extended-marriage. Tewahedo eschatology cites Lk 20:27-40 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the resurrection is the trans-marital + trans-procreative life of the Kingdom, distinct from earthly marriage's covenantal exclusivity.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'Neither can they die any more: for they are equal unto the angels; and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection' (Lk 20:36), Cyril reads the isaggelos (equal-to-angels) and the children-of-resurrection compound title as the canonical Lukan anchor of the resurrection-anthropology: the resurrected human is not made into an angel (against later Origenist confusion), but enjoys angelic immortality and angelic non-procreative communal-life. Tewahedo monastic theology cites Lk 20:36 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the bahǝtawi's celibacy anticipates the resurrection-state in this life — eschatological-existence proleptically embodied.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him' (Lk 20:38), Cyril reads the all-live-unto-him (pantes gar autō zōsin — Luke's distinctive addition over Mark/Matthew) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the patriarchs whom God identifies himself with (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) are alive-to-God right now — not merely scheduled-for-future-resurrection. The intermediate-state of the righteous is conscious-life-with-God. Tewahedo intermediate-state-theology cites Lk 20:38 as the canonical Lukan anchor doubled with Lk 16:23 (Lazarus in Abraham's bosom) and Lk 23:43 (today thou shalt be with me in paradise) — the conscious-life-with-Christ of the departed righteous is canonically witnessed three-times in Luke alone.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's puzzle from Psalm 110 — 'David himself saith in the book of Psalms, The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand' (Lk 20:42, citing Ps 110:1) — Cyril reads the Psalm-110 citation as the canonical Lukan anchor of the Christological double-Lordship: David (the messiah's ancestor) addresses the messiah AS HIS LORD, which makes the messiah more than merely David's son. Ps 110:1 becomes the most-cited Old-Testament verse in the New Testament (~25 times) and the foundational text for Christ's session at the Father's right hand (Ascension theology). Tewahedo Christology cites Lk 20:42 + Ps 110:1 as the canonical Old-Testament-Christological double-Lordship anchor; the Tewahedo Anaphora preserves the right-hand-of-the-Father language verbatim.

'This poor widow hath cast in more than they all' — Cyril reads the widow's mite as the canonical anchor of the all-or-nothing form of Christian almsgiving: the gift is measured not by the amount given but by the proportion of one's substance, and the widow who gives her last two coins gives literally everything. Tewahedo monastic voluntary poverty draws on Lk 21:3-4 as one of its earliest canonical anchors of total renunciation.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ANATHEMA anything laid up or suspended; hence anything laid up in a temple or set apart as sacred. In this sense the form of the word is anath(ee)ma, once in plural used in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 21:5, where it is rendered “gifts.” In the LXX. the form anathema is generally used as the rendering of the Hebrew word herem, derived from a verb which means (1) to consecrate or devote; and (2) to exterminate. Any object so devoted to the Lord could not be redeemed (Numbers 18:14; Leviticus 27:28, 29); and hence the idea of exterminating connected with the word. The Hebrew verb (haram) is frequently used of the extermination of idolatrous nations. It had a wide range of application. The anathema or herem was a person or thing irrevocably devoted to God (Leviticus 27:21, 28); and “none devoted shall be ransomed. He shall surely be put to death” (27:29). The word therefore carried the idea of devoted to destruction (Numbers 21:2, 3; Joshua 6:17); and hence generally it meant a thing accursed. In Deuteronomy 7:26 an idol is called a herem = anathema, a thing accursed. In the New Testament this word always implies execration. In some cases an individual denounces an anathema on himself unless certain conditions are fulfilled (Acts 23:12, 14, 21). “To call Jesus accursed” [anathema] (1 Corinthians 12:3) is to pronounce him execrated or accursed. If any one preached another gospel, the apostle says, “let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8, 9); i.e., let his conduct in so doing be accounted accursed. In Romans 9:3, the expression “accursed” (anathema) from Christ, i.e., excluded from fellowship or alliance with Christ, has occasioned much difficulty. The apostle here does not speak of his wish as a possible thing. It is simply a vehement expression of feeling, showing how strong was his desire for the salvation of his people. The anathema in 1 Corinthians 16:22 denotes simply that they who love not the Lord are rightly objects of loathing and execration to all holy beings; they are guilty of a crime that merits the severest condemnation; they are exposed to the just sentence of “everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord.”

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's prophecy 'there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down' (Lk 21:6), Cyril reads the Temple-destruction prophecy as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the canonical-end-of-the-Old-Covenant-cultus: the Temple as the chosen-place (Deu 12:5) is replaced by the eucharistic-altar in every local church. The destruction in 70 AD is the historical confirmation, but the spiritual transition is already accomplished in Christ. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Lk 21:6 + Heb 10 (sacrificial-system fulfilled in Christ's one offering) as the canonical doubled-witness for the New-Covenant transition; the tabot bearing the Christic-presence replaces the Temple as the dwelling of God.

On Christ's 'when ye shall hear of wars and commotions, be not terrified... the end is not by and by' (Lk 21:9), Cyril reads the not-by-and-by (ouk eutheōs — 'not immediately') qualification as the canonical Lukan anchor against eschatological-panic: military-and-political upheaval does NOT mean the end is now. Cyril notes the eschatological discourses regularly correct panic — Christian eschatology is patient, not feverish. Tewahedo eschatological-spirituality cites Lk 21:9 + 2 Th 2:1-2 (Pauline corrective against 'the day of the Lord is at hand' panic) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of patient-eschatological-hope rather than panic-eschatology.

On Christ's promise 'I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist' (Lk 21:15), Cyril reads the doubled-gift (mouth-and-wisdom) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the Spirit's-utterance-in-persecution: when the disciple is delivered up before kings, the Spirit speaks IN him. The doctrine flows into Stephen's defense before the Sanhedrin (Acts 6:10 — 'they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake'). Tewahedo confessor-theology cites Lk 21:15 + Acts 6:10 as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of the Spirit-given confessor's-utterance; the Tewahedo martyrs (e.g. Ethiopian Christians under Imperial persecution) participate in this canonical promise.

On Christ's 'But there shall not an hair of your head perish' (Lk 21:18), Cyril reads the hyperbolic-hair-promise in juxtaposition with the immediately-preceding 'some of you shall they cause to be put to death' (21:16) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the spiritual-preservation-through-bodily-death: the believer who dies for Christ does not perish (the hair-of-the-head is not lost) — the apparent perishing is preserved-life in the heavenly economy. Tewahedo martyr-theology cites Lk 21:18 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of resurrection-preservation: every hair of the Tewahedo martyrs (Saint Yared, the Nine Saints, Imperial-era confessors) is preserved with God.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled' (Lk 21:24), Cyril reads the times-of-the-Gentiles (kairoi ethnōn) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the Gentile-inclusion-interval: between the canonical-rejection of Christ at Calvary and the eschatological-restoration there is an apostolic-missionary period during which the Gentile-Ethiopian-nations are brought into the fold. Tewahedo missionary-eschatology cites Lk 21:24 + Rom 11:25 ('blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in') as the canonical Lukan-Pauline doubled-witness for the doctrine of the Tewahedo-Gentile-times — the Tewahedo Church's mission contributes to the fulfilment of the times of the Gentiles.

On Christ's 'when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh' (Lk 21:28), Cyril reads the doubled-imperative (look-up + lift-up-your-heads) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of upward-eschatological-orientation: the Christian's posture in eschatological-troubled-times is not downcast fear but upward-confident expectation. The redemption (apolytrōsis) draws-near is in present-tense participial form — the deliverance is approaching, not merely imminent. Tewahedo liturgical-posture cites Lk 21:28 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of standing-with-uplifted-eyes during the Eucharistic anaphora — the liturgical-posture embodies the eschatological-anticipation.

The stand-before-the-Son-of-Man is the canonical Lukan formula for eschatological-judgment-readiness. Tewahedo monastic-vigil-prayer (the night-office tradition of the great monasteries) cites Lk 21:36 + Lk 18:1 as the canonical doubled-Lukan-anchor for the ceaseless-prayer + eschatological-vigilance discipline.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer' (Lk 22:15), Cyril reads the Hebraic-redoubled-formula (epithymia epethymēsa) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's deliberate-eager-anticipation of the institutional Last Supper: not reluctant, not pressured, but deeply-desired. The Lord's eagerness for the canonical-eucharistic-institution dignifies every later celebration. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Lk 22:15 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's desire-for-the-eucharist; every Tewahedo Mass is participation in the Lord's own canonical-desire-fulfilment.

'This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me' — Cyril treats the Lukan institution narrative as the canonical anchor of his entire eucharistic theology: that the bread broken IS the body of Christ, that the body of Christ given for the believers is the same body born of the Virgin, that the Eucharist is the ongoing communication of the life-giving flesh of the Word. Tewahedo Anaphora cites Lk 22:19 as one of its principal canonical warrants of the real presence.

On Christ's 'This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you' (Lk 22:20), Cyril reads the new-testament-in-my-blood as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the eucharistic-cup-as-new-covenant-blood: the Lord identifies the wine as the cup of the New-Covenant ratified by his impending blood-shedding. The pairing of the bread-body (Lk 22:19 — seed entry) and the cup-blood-covenant institutes the full eucharistic-form. Tewahedo Anaphora theology cites Lk 22:20 + 1 Cor 11:25 as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of the cup as the new-covenant-blood; the Tewahedo Mass preserves Christ's covenant-blood institution language verbatim in every Anaphora.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). NEW TESTAMENT (Luke 22:20), rather “New Covenant,” in contrast to the old covenant of works, which is superseded. “The covenant of grace is called new; it succeeds to the old broken covenant of works. It is ever fresh, flourishing, and excellent; and under the gospel it is dispensed in a more clear, spiritual, extensive, and powerful manner than of old” (Brown of Haddington). Hence is derived the name given to the latter portion of the Bible. (See TESTAMENT.)

On the disciples' Last-Supper strife — 'there was also a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest' (Lk 22:24) — Cyril reads the strife-at-the-Last-Supper as the canonical Lukan anti-anchor: the very moment of institution, when the Word made flesh is on the verge of his death, the disciples argue about greatness. Christ's response (22:26-27 — 'I am among you as he that serveth') makes priestly-service the inversion of secular-greatness. Tewahedo episcopal-formation cites Lk 22:24-27 + Jn 13:14 (foot-washing) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of the bishop-as-servant — the highest ecclesial office is the lowest service-vocation.

On Christ's 'Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat' (Lk 22:31), Cyril reads the doubled-name (Simon, Simon) + the sifting-permission as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Satan's limited-permission-to-test (parallel to Job 1:6-12 + Lk 4:13 'the devil... departed from him for a season'): the testing is permitted, not unconstrained. The doubled-name-vocative is the same intimate-pastoral-form Christ uses with Martha (Lk 10:41), Saul (Acts 9:4), and at Gethsemane (Mt 26:38 — 'My soul is exceeding sorrowful'). Tewahedo pastoral theology cites Lk 22:31 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of pastoral-warning love: Christ warns Peter before the fall.

On Christ's 'But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren' (Lk 22:32), Cyril reads the doubled-promise (I-prayed-for-thee + strengthen-thy-brethren) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of dominical-intercession + apostolic-fraternity: Christ's High-Priestly intercession precedes the apostolic ministry; Peter's restoration is the model for fraternal-strengthening after each apostolic failure. Tewahedo pastoral-theology of confession cites Lk 22:32 as the canonical Lukan anchor for the priestly post-confession ministry — the restored confessor strengthens his brethren by sharing his repentance-and-restoration testimony.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GETHSEMANE oil-press, the name of an olive-yard at the foot of the Mount of Olives, to which Jesus was wont to retire (Luke 22:39) with his disciples, and which is specially memorable as being the scene of his agony (Mark 14:32; John 18:1; Luke 22:44). The plot of ground pointed out as Gethsemane is now surrounded by a wall, and is laid out as a modern European flower-garden. It contains eight venerable olive-trees, the age of which cannot, however, be determined. The exact site of Gethsemane is still in question. Dr. Thomson (The Land and the Book) says: “When I first came to Jerusalem, and for many years afterward, this plot of ground was open to all whenever they chose to come and meditate beneath its very old olivetrees. The Latins, however, have within the last few years succeeded in gaining sole possession, and have built a high wall around it...The Greeks have invented another site a little to the north of it...My own impression is that both are wrong. The position is too near the city, and so close to what must have always been the great thoroughfare eastward, that our Lord would scarcely have selected it for retirement on that dangerous and dismal night...I am inclined to place the garden in the secluded vale several hundred yards to the north-east of the present Gethsemane.”

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's Gethsemane prayer 'Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done' (Lk 22:42), Cyril reads the not-my-will-but-thine as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's two-wills in the unity of the one-person: the human-will of Christ truly desires deliverance, the divine-will (shared with the Father) wills the salvific-Passion. The hypostatic-union does not absorb the human will but ratifies its perfect-obedient-subordination to the divine. Tewahedo Christology — Miaphysite-with-two-operations — cites Lk 22:42 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that Christ in his humanity prays the prayer the entire human race must learn to pray: 'not my will but thine'.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the Lukan-unique addition 'And there appeared an angel unto him from heaven, strengthening him' (Lk 22:43), Cyril reads the Gethsemane-angel-strengthening as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of angelic-ministry to Christ in his true-human extremity: the same angels that ministered to him after the Temptation (Mt 4:11) now minister at the Passion's edge. The Word made flesh receives angelic strengthening — not because the divinity needs it, but because the humanity legitimately does. Tewahedo angelology cites Lk 22:43 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of angelic-ministry to suffering Christians; the Tewahedo Angelic-Intercession tradition (the 'Mäshafä Mäla'ǝkt' supplications) draws on this canonical pattern.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

'His sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground' — Cyril treats the Gethsemane sweat as the canonical anchor of the Lord's true humanity: the agony is real, the prayer is real, the consenting will is real. Against any Apollinarian reduction of the human will, Cyril insists that the Word in his humanity wills our salvation through real prayer to the Father. Tewahedo Holy-Thursday lectionary preserves Lk 22:44 as the canonical anchor of the Lord's prayerful humanity.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's word to the arresting-officers 'this is your hour, and the power of darkness' (Lk 22:53), Cyril reads the doubled-phrase (your-hour + power-of-darkness) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Satan-permitted-darkness-hour: the Passion proceeds not because Christ is defeated but because the Father permits the hour of the powers-of-darkness. The exousia tou skotous (authority of darkness) is the same authority Christ acknowledges at his arrest as permitted but not victorious. Tewahedo Holy-Week theology cites Lk 22:53 + Col 1:13 (delivered from the power of darkness) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the Cross goes through the darkness-hour to the resurrection-light.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HALL (Gr. aule, Luke 22:55; R.V., “court”), the open court or quadrangle belonging to the high priest’s house. In Matthew 26:69 and Mark 14:66 this word is incorrectly rendered “palace” in the Authorized Version, but correctly “court” in the Revised Version. In John 10:1,16 it means a “sheep-fold.” In Matthew 27:27 and Mark 15:16 (A.V., “common hall;” R.V., “palace”) it refers to the proetorium or residence of the Roman governor at Jerusalem. The “porch” in Matthew 26:71 is the entrance-hall or passage leading into the central court, which is open to the sky.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GALILEAN an inhabitant or native of Galilee. This word was used as a name of contempt as applied to our Lord’s disciples (Luke 22:59; Acts 2:7). All the apostles, with the exception of Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:11), were Galileans. Peter was detected by his Galilean accent (Matthew 26:69; Mark 14:70). This was also one of the names of reproach given to the early Christians. Julian the Apostate, as he is called, not only used the epithet himself when referring to Christ and his apostles, but he made it a law that no one should ever call the Christians by any other name.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Peter's Lukan-distinctive response after the cock-crow — 'And Peter went out, and wept bitterly' (Lk 22:62) — Cyril reads the eklausen pikrōs (wept bitterly) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of repentant-tears as the active-receptive expression of post-fall sorrow: tears are not despair but the moisture of returning-love. Peter's tears are the inverse of Judas's hanging (Mt 27:5); the same betrayal, different response. Tewahedo penitential theology cites Lk 22:62 + 2 Cor 7:10 (godly sorrow worketh repentance) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of repentant-tears; the Tewahedo monastic 'gift of tears' (charisma of compunction) is the spiritual descendant of Peter's Lukan tears.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PILATE , PONTIUS probably connected with the Roman family of the Pontii, and called “Pilate” from the Latin pileatus, i.e., “wearing the pileus”, which was the “cap or badge of a manumitted slave,” as indicating that he was a “freedman,” or the descendant of one. He was the sixth in the order of the Roman procurators of Judea (A.D. 26-36). His headquarters were at Caesarea, but he frequently went up to Jerusalem. His reign extended over the period of the ministry of John the Baptist and of Jesus Christ, in connection with whose trial his name comes into prominent notice. Pilate was a “typical Roman, not of the antique, simple stamp, but of the imperial period, a man not without some remains of the ancient Roman justice in his soul, yet pleasure-loving, imperious, and corrupt. He hated the Jews whom he ruled, and in times of irritation freely shed their blood. They returned his hatred with cordiality, and accused him of every crime, maladministration, cruelty, and robbery. He visited Jerusalem as seldom as possible; for, indeed, to one accustomed to the pleasures of Rome, with its theatres, baths, games, and gay society, Jerusalem, with its religiousness and ever-smouldering revolt, was a dreary residence. When he did visit it he stayed in the palace of Herod the Great, it being common for the officers sent by Rome into conquered countries to occupy the palaces of the displaced sovereigns.” After his trial before the Sanhedrin, Jesus was brought to the Roman procurator, Pilate, who had come up to Jerusalem as usual to preserve order during the Passover, and was now residing, perhaps, in the castle of Antonia, or it may be in Herod’s palace. Pilate came forth from his palace and met the deputation from the Sanhedrin, who, in answer to his inquiry as to the nature of the accusation they had to prefer against Jesus, accused him of being a “malefactor.” Pilate was not satisfied with this, and they further accused him (1) of sedition, (2) preventing the payment of the tribute to Caesar, and (3) of assuming the title of king (Luke 23:2). Pilate now withdrew with Jesus into the palace (John 18:33) and examined him in private (37,38); and then going out to the deputation still standing before the gate, he declared that he could find no fault in Jesus (Luke 23:4). This only aroused them to more furious clamour, and they cried that he excited the populace “throughout all Jewry, beginning from Galilee.” When Pilate heard of Galilee, he sent the accused to Herod Antipas, who had jurisdiction over that province, thus hoping to escape the difficulty in which he found himself. But Herod, with his men of war, set Jesus at nought, and sent him back again to Pilate, clad in a purple robe of mockery (23:11, 12). Pilate now proposed that as he and Herod had found no fault in him, they should release Jesus; and anticipating that they would consent to this proposal, he ascended the judgment-seat as if ready to ratify the decision (Matthew 27:19). But at this moment his wife (Claudia Procula) sent a message to him imploring him to have nothing to do with the “just person.” Pilate’s feelings of perplexity and awe were deepened by this incident, while the crowd vehemently cried out, “Not this man, but Barabbas.” Pilate answered, “What then shall I do with Jesus?” The fierce cry immediately followed. “Let him be crucified.” Pilate, apparently vexed, and not knowning what to do, said, “Why, what evil hath he done?” but with yet fiercer fanaticism the crowd yelled out, “Away with him! crucify him, crucify him!” Pilate yielded, and sent Jesus away to be scourged. This scourging was usually inflicted by lictors; but as Pilate was only a procurator he had no lictor, and hence his soldiers inflicted this terrible punishment. This done, the soldiers began to deride the sufferer, and they threw around him a purple robe, probably some old cast-off robe of state (Matthew 27:28; John 19:2), and putting a reed in his right hand, and a crowd of thorns on his head, bowed the knee before him in mockery, and saluted him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” They took also the reed and smote him with it on the head and face, and spat in his face, heaping upon him every indignity. Pilate then led forth Jesus from within the Praetorium (Matthew 27:27) before the people, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe, saying, “Behold the man!” But the sight of Jesus, now scourged and crowned and bleeding, only stirred their hatred the more, and again they cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” and brought forth this additional charge against him, that he professed to be “the Son of God.” Pilate heard this accusation with a superstitious awe, and taking him once more within the Praetorium, asked him, “Whence art thou?” Jesus gave him no answer. Pilate was irritated by his continued silence, and said, “Knowest thou not that I have power to crucify thee?” Jesus, with calm dignity, answered the Roman, “Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above.” After this Pilate seemed more resolved than ever to let Jesus go. The crowd perceiving this cried out, “If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar’s friend.” This settled the matter. He was afraid of being accused to the emperor. Calling for water, he washed his hands in the sight of the people, saying, “I am innocent of the blood of this just person.” The mob, again scorning his scruples, cried, “His blood be on us, and on our children.” Pilate was stung to the heart by their insults, and putting forth Jesus before them, said, “Shall I crucify your King?” The fatal moment had now come. They madly exclaimed, “We have no king but Caesar;” and now Jesus is given up to them, and led away to be crucified. By the direction of Pilate an inscription was placed, according to the Roman custom, over the cross, stating the crime for which he was crucified. Having ascertained from the centurion that he was dead, he gave up the body to Joseph of Arimathea to be buried. Pilate’s name now disappears from the Gospel history. References to him, however, are found in the Acts of the Apostles (3:13; 4:27; 13:28), and in 1 Timothy 6:13. In A.D. 36 the governor of Syria brought serious accusations against Pilate, and he was banished to Vienne in Gaul, where, according to tradition, he committed suicide.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ANTIPAS (1.) Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great by his Samaritan wife Malthace. He was tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea during the whole period of our Lord’s life on earth (Luke 23:7). He was a frivolous and vain prince, and was chargeable with many infamous crimes (Mark 8:15; Luke 3:19; 13:31, 32). He beheaded John the Baptist (Matthew 14:1-12) at the instigation of Herodias, the wife of his half-brother Herod-Philip, whom he had married. Pilate sent Christ to him when he was at Jerusalem at the Passover (Luke 23:7). He asked some idle questions of him, and after causing him to be mocked, sent him back again to Pilate. The wife of Chuza, his house-steward, was one of our Lord’s disciples (Luke 8:3). (2.) A “faithful martyr” (Revelation 2:13), of whom nothing more is certainly known.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the Jerusalem-mob's cry 'Crucify him, crucify him' (Lk 23:21), Cyril reads the doubled-imperative as the canonical Lukan anchor of the canonical-prophetic-rejection's voice: the cry that reverses the Hosanna of Lk 19:38 by the same population. Cyril is careful to distinguish the city-political mob from 'the Jewish people' as a whole (against any later anti-Judaic reading); the cry is the act of a Jerusalem-Caiaphas-orchestrated faction. Tewahedo pastoral theology cites Lk 23:21 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the same human voice can ascribe Hosanna-and-Crucify within a single week — the warning against fickle-religiosity.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's word to the Lukan-distinctive 'daughters of Jerusalem' — 'Weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children' (Lk 23:28) — Cyril reads the redirected-tears as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of properly-ordered-sorrow: the Christian does not pity the Crucified (he chose the Cross) but laments his/her own sin (whose burden he bears). The prophetic-Tewahedo lamentation tradition (the bēbet-äbiyot procession of Holy Week) preserves the redirected-sorrow pattern: the weeping is for our sins, not Christ's death. Tewahedo Holy-Week theology cites Lk 23:28 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of redirected-Holy-Week-lament.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). THIEVES , THE TWO (Luke 23:32, 39-43), robbers, rather brigands, probably followers of Barabbas. Our Lord’s cross was placed between those of the “malefactors,” to add to the ignominy of his position. According to tradition, Demas or Dismas was the name of the penitent thief hanging on the right, and Gestas of the impenitent on the left.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the place-name 'Calvary' (Lk 23:33 — kranion 'place of a skull'), Cyril reads the Hebrew-Aramaic Golgotha as the canonical Lukan anchor of the typological-doctrine that the place of Christ's death is the symbolic place of Adam's skull: the Adamic-tradition (preserved in Tewahedo Synaxarium and Mäshafä-Adam) locates Adam's burial at Golgotha, making Christ's blood flow over the first father's bones. Tewahedo iconography cites Lk 23:33 + the Mäshafä-Adam tradition as the canonical doubled-witness for the depictive-tradition of the Adamic-skull at the foot of the Cross — the Cross stands over the head of the first father; the Second Adam restores what the First Adam lost.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CALVARY only in Luke 23:33, the Latin name Calvaria, which was used as a translation of the Greek word Kranion, by which the Hebrew word Gulgoleth was interpreted, “the place of a skull.” It probably took this name from its shape, being a hillock or low, rounded, bare elevation somewhat in the form of a human skull. It is nowhere in Scripture called a “hill.” The crucifixion of our Lord took place outside the city walls (Hebrews 13:11-13) and near the public thoroughfare. “This thing was not done in a corner.” (See GOLGOTHA.)

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do' — Cyril treats the first word from the Cross as the canonical fulfilment of Is 53:12 ('he made intercession for the transgressors'). The intercessory office of the High Priest is exercised from the altar of the Cross itself. The 'they know not' is a real plea for ignorance-extenuation: those who execute Christ are bidden to the same forgiveness offered to all. Tewahedo Good-Friday liturgy preserves Lk 23:34 at the head of the seven words.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). INTERCESSION OF CHRIST Christ’s priestly office consists of these two parts, (1) the offering up of himself as a sacrifice, and (2) making continual intercession for us. When on earth he made intercession for his people (Luke 23:34; John 17:20; Hebrews 5:7); but now he exercises this function of his priesthood in heaven, where he is said to appear in the presence of God for us (Hebrews 9:12,24). His advocacy with the Father for his people rests on the basis of his own all-perfect sacrifice. Thus he pleads for and obtains the fulfilment of all the promises of the everlasting covenant (1 John 2:1; John 17:24; Hebrews 7:25). He can be “touched with the feeling of our infirmities,” and is both a merciful and a faithful high priest (Hebrews 2:17, 18; 4:15, 16). This intercession is an essential part of his mediatorial work. Through him we have “access” to the Father (John 14:6; Ephesians 2:18; 3:12). “The communion of his people with the Father will ever be sustained through him as mediatorial Priest” (Psalm 110:4; Revelation 7:17).

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the cross-superscription 'THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS' (Lk 23:38 — in Greek, Latin, Hebrew per Jn 19:20), Cyril reads the trilingual-titulus as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the universal-kingship-of-Christ proclaimed at the Cross: Pilate's intended-mockery becomes (against his intent) the canonical proclamation of Christ's kingship in the three languages of the known world (Hebrew = covenantal, Greek = cultural, Latin = imperial). Tewahedo Solomonic-dynasty self-understanding cites Lk 23:38 + Jn 19:20 as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the King of the Jews is also the King of all nations — the Ethiopian Solomonic-dynastic claim to Christ-the-King derives from this universal-trilingual-titulus.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the good-thief's plea 'Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom' (Lk 23:42), Cyril reads the dying-thief's confession as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of last-moment-saving-faith: a sinner with no time for catechesis, no baptism, no works — yet his confession ('Lord' + recognition of the kingdom) suffices. Christ's answer (Lk 23:43 — seed entry) is the canonical promise; this verse is the canonical confession. Tewahedo pastoral-theology of last-rites cites Lk 23:42 + Lk 23:43 as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness for the doctrine that the deathbed confession is salvifically-effective; the priest at the bedside follows the dominical pattern of the Christ-and-thief exchange.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

'Today shalt thou be with me in paradise' — Cyril reads the promise to the good thief as the canonical anchor of three doctrines: (1) Christ retains the prerogative of paradise even at the moment of his apparent defeat; (2) confession-from-the-cross suffices for salvation; (3) the saints enter paradise immediately at death and do not wait. The 'today' rules out every reading that defers the saints' beatific reception to the Last Day alone. Tewahedo intermediate-state doctrine cites Lk 23:43 as a principal canonical anchor.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PARADISE a Persian word (pardes), properly meaning a “pleasure-ground” or “park” or “king’s garden.” (See EDEN.) It came in course of time to be used as a name for the world of happiness and rest hereafter (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 12:4; Revelation 2:7). For “garden” in Genesis 2:8 the LXX. has “paradise.”

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the cosmic-darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour (Lk 23:44), Cyril reads the three-hour-darkness as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the cosmic-participation in the Passion: creation darkens because its Maker dies. The three hours echo Jonah's three days in the fish (Mt 12:40), the three days Moses was in the ark (Jub 47:5), and the three days Christ will be in the tomb. Tewahedo cosmic-Christology cites Lk 23:44 + Mt 27:51-52 (earth-quake, rocks rent, graves opened) as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the natural-cosmic-order participates in the death of its Word-Maker; the Tewahedo Holy-Friday liturgy preserves the three-hour darkening observance.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the Temple-veil rent in twain at Christ's death (Lk 23:45), Cyril reads the schism-of-the-veil as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the opening-of-access to the Holy-of-Holies through Christ's flesh (Heb 10:19-20 — 'a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh'). The veil rent from top to bottom (Mt 27:51) signals God's-direction rather than human-direction of the action. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Lk 23:45 + Heb 10:19-20 as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that the iconographic-curtain in the Tewahedo sanctuary (which veils the maqdas) functions as both barrier-and-passage — the curtain that screens is also the curtain that opens at the Eucharistic moment.

'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit' — Cyril treats the Lukan death-cry, drawn from Ps 31:5, as the canonical anchor of every Christian's death-bed prayer: the soul is commended to the Father who created it, by the same words the eternal Son used. The Word does not lose his divinity at the cry of dereliction; the soul-Father committal is the calm answer to the Markan-Matthean cry. Tewahedo funeral office cites Lk 23:46 as the canonical commendation-prayer.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Joseph of Arimathea's wrapping of Christ's body and burial 'in a sepulchre that was hewn in stone, wherein never man before was laid' (Lk 23:53), Cyril reads the new-unused-tomb as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the sanctified-tomb: just as the virgin-womb prepared the Word's entry into the world, the new-tomb (Joseph's own, never used) prepares his three-day rest. The pairing virgin-womb + new-tomb forms the canonical-bookend of the Incarnation. Tewahedo Marian-and-Easter theology cites Lk 23:53 + Lk 1:34-35 ('how shall this be, seeing I know not a man') as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of the sanctified-virginal-spaces that bound the Incarnation.

On the women's discovery 'upon the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they came unto the sepulchre' (Lk 24:1), Cyril reads the first-day-of-the-week (mia tōn sabbatōn) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the resurrection's calendrical-establishment of the Lord's-Day: the resurrection inaugurates the new-creation week, and the first-day becomes the Christian sabbath (without abolishing the Saturday-Sabbath — Tewahedo preserves BOTH per Acts 20:7 + Heb 4:9). Tewahedo doubled-Sabbath-observance cites Lk 24:1 + Acts 20:7 + Jub 50:9 (Saturday-Sabbath as foretaste of the holy kingdom) as the canonical triple-witness for the Tewahedo Sänbatä-Krǝstiyan (Christian-Sabbath) on Sunday alongside the Saturday Sabbath.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the angels' question to the women 'Why seek ye the living among the dead?' (Lk 24:5), Cyril reads the angelic-rhetorical-question as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the proper-place-of-the-living-Christ: the tomb is the wrong location for the living Lord. The angels redirect from tomb-search to risen-recognition. Tewahedo Easter (Fasika) liturgy cites Lk 24:5 + Lk 24:6 ('he is not here, but is risen') as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine that Easter-worship is not tomb-pilgrimage but risen-Christ-recognition; the Tewahedo Pascha vigil uses the angelic-question as a refrain.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the angels' recital of Christ's pre-Passion prediction — 'the Son of man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and the third day rise again' (Lk 24:7) — Cyril reads the dei (must-be) + third-day-rise as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the entire Passion + Resurrection sequence is divinely-necessary (the Lukan dei recurs at 9:22, 17:25, 22:37, 24:7, 24:26, 24:44 — six times the divine-necessity formula). The third-day-rise specifically fulfils Hos 6:2 + Jonah's three-days. Tewahedo Pascha theology cites Lk 24:7 + Hos 6:2 + Mt 12:40 as the canonical triple-witness of the divinely-necessary third-day-resurrection.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the Emmaus-road encounter (Lk 24:13-32), Cyril reads the unique-Lukan post-resurrection narrative as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the eucharistic-recognition pattern: word-of-Christ (expounded along the road, Lk 24:27) → breaking-of-bread (eyes opened, Lk 24:30-31 seed) → burning-hearts (in retrospect, Lk 24:32). The structure preserves the canonical Eucharistic shape: Liturgy of the Word + Liturgy of the Sacrament + Mystagogical reflection. Tewahedo Anaphora structure cites Lk 24:13-32 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the Eucharistic-recognition-shape; every Tewahedo Mass is an Emmaus-road journey.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). EMMAUS hot baths, a village “three-score furlongs” from jerusalem, where our Lord had an interview with two of his disciples on the day of his resurrection (Luke 24:13). This has been identified with the modern el-Kubeibeh, lying over 7 miles north-west of Jerusalem. This name, el-Kubeibeh, meaning “little dome,” is derived from the remains of the Crusaders’ church yet to be found there. Others have identified it with the modern Khurbet Khamasa i.e., “the ruins of Khamasa”, about 8 miles south-west of Jerusalem, where there are ruins also of a Crusaders’ church. Its site, however has been much disputed.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FURLONG a stadium, a Greek measure of distance equal to 606 feet and 9 inches (Luke 24:13; John 6:19; 11:18; Revelation 14:20; 21:16).

On the risen Christ's rebuke 'O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken' (Lk 24:25), Cyril reads the rebuke + 'all-that-the-prophets-have-spoken' as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the comprehensive-prophetic-witness to Christ: the Resurrection-Christ holds his disciples accountable to ALL the prophets, not selected proof-texts. The slow-of-heart-to-believe formula appears as a Lukan refrain (Lk 24:11 + 24:25 + 24:38). Tewahedo Bibliology cites Lk 24:25 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the unitary-prophetic-canon: the Old Testament prophets uniformly witness to Christ; selectivity or hesitance is rebuked.

On the Emmaus-road exposition 'And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself' (Lk 24:27), Cyril reads the comprehensive-Christological-hermeneutic as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the entire Old Testament is Christologically interpretable: the Lord himself models the patristic-Christological hermeneutic on the resurrection road. Cyril's own commentaries (and the entire patristic exegetical tradition) appropriate this canonical-resurrection-pattern as their methodological foundation. Tewahedo Andǝmta hermeneutic cites Lk 24:27 as the canonical Lukan anchor for the multi-layered Christological reading of the Tewahedo canonical Scriptures.

'He took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him' — Cyril reads the Emmaus recognition as the canonical Lukan disclosure that the Risen Christ is known IN the breaking of the bread. The same gesture that instituted the Eucharist on Holy Thursday opens the disciples' eyes on Easter evening. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Lk 24:30-31 as the canonical anchor that every Eucharist is an Emmaus-recognition.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the Emmaus-disciples' retrospective 'Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?' (Lk 24:32), Cyril reads the burning-heart formula as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the affective-pneumatological response to Scripture-rightly-expounded: the heart-burn is the Spirit's-confirmation of the Christological exegesis. The same heart-burn recurs at Pentecost (Acts 2:3 — 'cloven tongues like as of fire'). Tewahedo monastic-mystical theology cites Lk 24:32 + Acts 2:3 as the canonical doubled-witness for the doctrine of the Spirit-given heart-burn at canonical-Scripture-encounter; the Tewahedo daily Mass preserves the Word-and-Sacrament heart-burning pattern.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the risen Christ's 'Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have' (Lk 24:39), Cyril reads the handle-me + flesh-and-bones formula as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the real-bodily-resurrection: not a ghost, not a mere appearance, but a transformed-yet-real body with flesh-and-bones. The verse is load-bearing against the docetic-spiritualizing tendencies that would later challenge the resurrection. Tewahedo Easter theology cites Lk 24:39 + Jn 20:27 ('reach hither thy finger') + 1 Cor 15:42-44 (resurrection body) as the canonical triple-witness for the real-bodily-resurrection doctrine; the Tewahedo Fasika Anaphora confesses 'we believe in the resurrection of the body'.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HAGIOGRAPHA the holy writings, a term which came early into use in the Christian church to denote the third division of the Old Testament scriptures, called by the Jews Kethubim, i.e., “Writings.” It consisted of five books, viz., Job, Proverbs, and Psalms, and the two books of Chronicles. The ancient Jews classified their sacred books as the Law, the Prophets, and the Kethubim, or Writings. (See BIBLE.) In the New Testament (Luke 24:44) we find three corresponding divisions, viz., the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the risen Christ's final commission 'behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high' (Lk 24:49), Cyril reads the doubled-promise (promise-of-the-Father + power-from-on-high) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the Pentecost-anticipation: the Promise-of-the-Father is the Holy Spirit (cf. Acts 1:4-5, Acts 2:33), the power-from-on-high is the Spirit's-coming-down. The verse is the bridge from the Gospel of Luke to Acts; the same Spirit who descended on Christ at the Jordan (Lk 3:22) will descend on the Church at Pentecost. Tewahedo pneumatology cites Lk 24:49 + Acts 1:4-5 + Acts 2:1-4 as the canonical Lukan-Acts triple-witness for the Pentecostal Promise; the Tewahedo Pentecost feast (Pärräqlēṭos) preserves this canonical Lukan promise-fulfilment.

↩ ◇ Cyril of Alexandria (430). Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

'He was parted from them, and carried up into heaven' — Cyril treats the Lukan Ascension as the canonical inauguration of the Word-made-flesh's session at the Father's right hand: the same humanity assumed from the Virgin is enthroned in glory. The Ascension is not the departure of the Word from his flesh but the elevation of the flesh into the divine glory. Tewahedo Ascension feast (Ǝrgät) cites Lk 24:51 alongside Acts 1:9-11 as the canonical diptych of the heavenly enthronement.

Douay-Rheims

I pray not that thou shouldst take them out of the world, but that thou shouldst keep them from evil.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Arabic (Van Dyck)

et pro eis ego sanctifico meipsum: ut sint et ipsi sanctificati in veritate.

Greek (Byzantine Majority Text)

ut omnes unum sint, sicut tu Pater in me, et ego in te, ut et ipsi in nobis unum sint: ut credat mundus, quia tu me misisti.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

The Good News According to John 17:23.

وَآيَاتٍ أُخَرَ كَثِيرَةً صَنَعَ يَسُوعُ قُدَّامَ تَلَامِيذِهِ لَمْ تُكْتَبْ فِي هَذَا ٱلْكِتَابِ.

↩

The Good News According to John 20:31.

Greek (Byzantine Majority Text)

Arabic (Van Dyck)

بَعْدَ هَذَا أَظْهَرَ أَيْضًا يَسُوعُ نَفْسَهُ لِلتَّلَامِيذِ عَلَى بَحْرِ طَبَرِيَّةَ. ظَهَرَ هَكَذَا:

↩

The Good News According to John 21:2.

Greek (Byzantine Majority Text)

erant simul Simon Petrus, et Thomas, qui dicitur Didymus, et Nathanaël, qui erat a Cana Galilææ, et filii Zebedæi, et alii ex discipulis ejus duo.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

كَانَ سِمْعَانُ بُطْرُسُ، وَتُومَا ٱلَّذِي يُقَالُ لَهُ ٱلتَّوْأَمُ، وَنَثَنَائِيلُ ٱلَّذِي مِنْ قَانَا ٱلْجَلِيلِ، وَٱبْنَا زَبْدِي، وَٱثْنَانِ آخَرَانِ مِنْ تَلَامِيذِهِ مَعَ بَعْضِهِمْ.

↩

The Good News According to John 21:3.

Greek (Byzantine Majority Text)

Arabic (Van Dyck)

قَالَ لَهُمْ سِمْعَانُ بُطْرُسُ: «أَنَا أَذْهَبُ لِأَتَصَيَّدَ». قَالُوا لَهُ: «نَذْهَبُ نَحْنُ أَيْضًا مَعَكَ». فَخَرَجُوا وَدَخَلُوا ٱلسَّفِينَةَ لِلْوَقْتِ. وَفِي تِلْكَ ٱللَّيْلَةِ لَمْ يُمْسِكُوا شَيْئًا.

↩

The Good News According to John 21:4.

Greek (Byzantine Majority Text)

Douay-Rheims

But when the morning was come, Jesus stood on the shore: yet the disciples knew not that it was Jesus.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

↩

The Good News According to John 21:5.

Greek (Byzantine Majority Text)

Douay-Rheims

Arabic (Van Dyck)

The Good News According to John 21:6.

Greek (Byzantine Majority Text)

The Good News According to John 21:7.

↩

The Good News According to John 21:17.

He saith unto him the third time, Simon, [son] of Jonas, lovest thou me? Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me? And he said unto him, Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee. Jesus saith unto him, Feed my sheep.

Greek (Byzantine Majority Text)

Douay-Rheims

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)
